tools.name: SuggestSkills
tools.description:
Render a card of standalone skills the user can add — org, shared, or Anthropic skills not yet enabled.

Call this when the task is one a skill could make repeatable — drafting in a house style, reviews against a playbook, a recurring workflow — and nothing enabled covers it; the user does not need to ask about skills. Also when they ask for recommendations, or when ListSkills returned zero matches. Use ListSkills for skills they already have.

Do NOT call this for one-off questions you can answer directly, when you are unsure a skill would help, or if you already rendered a suggestion this conversation and the user didn't engage.

Pass keywords drawn from the task itself, and set trigger ('proactive' when you initiated this from task context, 'user_asked' when they asked). If the result is empty and the trigger was proactive, continue the task without mentioning that you searched; if the user asked, tell them you found nothing new to add.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__dismiss_task
tools.description:
Withdraw a background-task chip you previously created with spawn_task.

Call this when a suggestion you flagged is now stale, superseded, or irrelevant — e.g. you (or the user) already fixed it in this session, or you spawned a better-scoped replacement. To replace a chip: call spawn_task with the new suggestion first, then dismiss the old task_id.

Only chips the user hasn't acted on can be withdrawn from the queue. If the user already started or dismissed the task, the result says so (a dismissed task's copy kept for later is withdrawn too) — do not retry.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__mark_chapter
tools.description:
Mark the start of a new chapter in this session.

Call this when the work shifts to a meaningfully different phase — e.g. after finishing exploration and starting implementation, after a fix lands and you move to verification, or when the user pivots to an unrelated request. The user sees a divider in the transcript and a floating table of contents for jumping between chapters.

Use sparingly: a chapter should cover a coherent stretch of work, not every tool call. A typical session has 3–8 chapters. Do not mark a chapter for the very first message — the session start is implicit.

The title is a short noun phrase ("Codebase exploration", "Auth bug fix", "Test verification"), not a sentence.

tools.description:
Flag an out-of-scope issue for a separate background task.

Call this when you notice something worth fixing that would bloat the current change — dead code, stale docs, missing coverage, a confirmed TODO, or a security issue spotted in passing. Don't flag vague code-smell observations, trivial fixes you can do inline, or low-confidence hunches. A chip appears for the user; one click spins it off into its own session. Your current turn continues uninterrupted.

The prompt must stand alone — include file paths and enough context to act without this conversation.

The result includes a task_id; call dismiss_task with it if the suggestion later becomes stale.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__browser_batch
tools.description: Execute a sequence of Browser pane tool calls in ONE round trip. Each item is {name, input} where input is exactly what you'd pass to that tool standalone. Actions execute SEQUENTIALLY (not in parallel) and stop on the first error. Use this tool extensively to quickly execute work whenever you can predict two or more steps ahead — e.g. navigate, click a field, type, press Return, screenshot. Each tool's own permission check runs per item — a step on a site the user hasn't allowed either asks the user inline (and continues if they allow) or is refused, which stops the batch; if a step is refused for a missing permission, call that tool on its own (that call can ask the user), then batch the rest. Screenshots and other images are returned interleaved with outputs; coordinates you write in THIS batch refer to the screenshot taken BEFORE this call. browser_batch cannot be nested, and preview_start is not batchable — but if the Browser pane isn't open yet, a batch whose FIRST action is navigate with a url opens it (other actions still need an open page).

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
tools.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

schema.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
schema.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

action.description:
The action to perform:
* `left_click`: Click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `right_click`: Click the right mouse button at the specified coordinates to open context menus.
* `double_click`: Double-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `triple_click`: Triple-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `type`: Type a string of text.
* `screenshot`: Take a screenshot of the screen.
* `wait`: Wait for a specified number of seconds.
* `scroll`: Scroll up, down, left, or right at the specified coordinates.
* `key`: Press a specific keyboard key.
* `left_click_drag`: Drag from start_coordinate to coordinate.
* `zoom`: Take a screenshot of a specific region for closer inspection.
* `scroll_to`: Scroll an element into view using its element reference ID from read_page or find tools.
* `hover`: Move the mouse cursor to the specified coordinates or element without clicking. Useful for revealing tooltips, dropdown menus, or triggering hover states.

coordinate.description: (x, y): The x (pixels from the left edge) and y (pixels from the top edge) coordinates. Required for `left_click`, `right_click`, `double_click`, `triple_click`, and `scroll`. For `left_click_drag`, this is the end position.

text.description: The text to type (for `type` action) or the key(s) to press (for `key` action). For `key` action: Provide space-separated keys (e.g., "Backspace Backspace Delete"). Supports keyboard shortcuts using the platform's modifier key (use "cmd" on Mac, "ctrl" on Windows/Linux, e.g., "cmd+a" or "ctrl+a" for select all). Page zoom shortcuts (e.g. "cmd+=", "ctrl+-", "cmd+0") are not supported - use the `zoom` action to magnify a region of the page instead.

duration.description: The number of seconds to wait. Required for `wait`. Maximum 10 seconds.

scroll_direction.description: The direction to scroll. Required for `scroll`.

scroll_amount.description: The number of scroll wheel ticks. Optional for `scroll`, defaults to 3.

region.description: (x0, y0, x1, y1): The rectangular region to capture for `zoom`. Coordinates define a rectangle from top-left (x0, y0) to bottom-right (x1, y1) in pixels from the viewport origin. Required for `zoom` action. Useful for inspecting small UI elements like icons, buttons, or text.

scale.description: For `screenshot` and `zoom` only. Scale factor in [0.1, 1] for the returned image; 1 (default) uses the full image token budget, 0.5 returns an image at half the width and height (~quarter of the tokens). Coordinates are ALWAYS in the full-resolution coordinate frame (reported with every scaled screenshot), never in the scaled image's own pixels.

repeat.description: Number of times to repeat the key sequence. Only applicable for `key` action. Must be a positive integer between 1 and 100. Default is 1. Useful for navigation tasks like pressing arrow keys multiple times.

ref.description: Element reference ID from read_page or find tools (e.g., "ref_1", "ref_2"). Required for `scroll_to` action. Can be used as alternative to `coordinate` for click actions.

modifiers.description: Modifier keys for click actions. Supports: "ctrl", "shift", "alt", "cmd" (or "meta"), "win" (or "windows"). Can be combined with "+" (e.g., "ctrl+shift", "cmd+alt"). Optional.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__resize_window
tools.description: Emulate a viewport size in the Browser pane tab. Presets: mobile (375x812), tablet (768x1024), or desktop, which clears the size emulation and returns the tab to the pane's own responsive size. Custom sizes need both width and height. An emulated size applies to that tab across reloads and navigation (scaled down to fit when it is larger than the pane): reset it with preset "desktop" as soon as you finish testing. The desktop app may also clear a size you set when your turn ends, so set it again in a later turn if you still need it. A size the user picked from the pane's own Viewport menu is theirs and stays until they or you change it; leave it unless they ask. colorScheme (light/dark) emulates prefers-color-scheme on that tab; it survives reloads and preset "desktop" does not touch it, but the pane re-syncs the tab to the app's light/dark theme when that theme changes or the pane reopens; local documents and static HTML previews always render light. The mobile preset (and any width < 768) also emulates a mobile device: Android Chrome user agent and 5 touch points, so pages detect a touch phone; your clicks still arrive as mouse clicks. Reload the page after switching so load-time device gates re-run.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Code_iOS_Simulator__control
tools.description: Run, test, and visually verify iOS apps in the iOS Simulator on this Mac. Use this whenever the user wants to see or try their iOS app — "run my app", "test this on iPhone", "does this look right?", "try the new screen" — not only when they mention the simulator by name. Simulator only: this tool cannot drive or stream a physical iPhone or iPad. If the user wants the app on their real device ("on my iPhone", "on my device"), build and deploy for the device with your normal build tools instead, and say the live panel only shows simulators. 'attach' opens a live panel so the user can watch — when the user wants to see the app, call 'attach' FIRST, before building: it is cheap, opens instantly on a booted simulator, and errors harmlessly when nothing is booted (boot or build, then retry it). 'launch' installs and launches a built .app — build it first, with the user's own build tooling or this server's 'build' tool when this session has it; launch re-attaches on its own, but do not rely on that instead of the early attach. Screenshots and tap/swipe/text verification are headless and need no panel. Don't open the panel when the user only asked to build/compile or to run unit tests. Coordinates are in device points (origin top-left); the 'launch' result reports the device's point dimensions.

schema.name: mcp__Claude_Code_iOS_Simulator__control
schema.description: Run, test, and visually verify iOS apps in the iOS Simulator on this Mac. Use this whenever the user wants to see or try their iOS app — "run my app", "test this on iPhone", "does this look right?", "try the new screen" — not only when they mention the simulator by name. Simulator only: this tool cannot drive or stream a physical iPhone or iPad. If the user wants the app on their real device ("on my iPhone", "on my device"), build and deploy for the device with your normal build tools instead, and say the live panel only shows simulators. 'attach' opens a live panel so the user can watch — when the user wants to see the app, call 'attach' FIRST, before building: it is cheap, opens instantly on a booted simulator, and errors harmlessly when nothing is booted (boot or build, then retry it). 'launch' installs and launches a built .app — build it first, with the user's own build tooling or this server's 'build' tool when this session has it; launch re-attaches on its own, but do not rely on that instead of the early attach. Screenshots and tap/swipe/text verification are headless and need no panel. Don't open the panel when the user only asked to build/compile or to run unit tests. Coordinates are in device points (origin top-left); the 'launch' result reports the device's point dimensions.

action.description: What to do. 'attach' opens the live simulator panel for the user — call it BEFORE you build or launch, as soon as the user wants to see the app: on a booted simulator it opens immediately, and otherwise it returns a clear, harmless error (boot or build first, then retry it). Do not skip the early attach because 'launch' also attaches — the panel should be open before the build starts. The panel is the user's view, not a precondition — 'screenshot' and input actions work without it. Skip it only when the user has no interest in watching; 'launch' installs and launches an .app (it also re-attaches, but call 'attach' early rather than relying on that); 'screenshot' returns a PNG of the current screen; 'inspect' returns the accessibility tree of the front app (what a screen reader reads, which can differ from what is drawn) as JSON — per element: type, label, value, frame [x,y,width,height] in device points from the top-left, traits the type does not imply, enabled only when false, children. Prefer it to 'screenshot' to find what to tap (tap a frame's center), read text, or check a control's state or value; use 'screenshot' for layout, color, and images. Default: the whole visible tree; x/y: the element under that point with its descendants (a point between controls hits their container); marker: the first element whose label (or match_key) contains that text. Hidden, off-screen, and illegibly small elements are omitted and counted, and text longer than its area shows is cut and ends with ... (occlusion and transparency are not detected); a tree over the size cap loses its deepest levels first and says so — narrow with x/y or marker; 'tap'/'swipe'/'text'/'button' inject input; 'touch_path' performs a single-finger drag along an arbitrary path (eased curves, long-press-then-drag); 'touch2_path' is the two-finger variant for pinch/rotate; 'open_url' opens a deep link; 'detach' closes the panel/stream. NOTE: a 'swipe' or 'touch_path' whose start point is on-screen and within 4pt of an edge performs the OS edge gesture instead of a plain drag — left=back, top=notification shade, bottom=home/app-switcher, right=Control Center (mapped to the current interface orientation). Start more than 4pt from the edge to drag or scroll content near the bezel.

app_path.description: For 'launch': path to the built .app bundle (e.g. DerivedData/.../Build/Products/Debug-iphonesimulator/MyApp.app).

device.description: Simulator name (e.g. 'iPhone 17 Pro') or UDID. Defaults to the currently attached simulator, or the first booted one. The first use of a device asks the user for permission.

udid.description: Alias for 'device' (identical semantics: simulator name or UDID). Pass at most one of 'device' / 'udid'.

bundle_id.description: For 'launch': bundle identifier. If omitted, extracted from the .app's Info.plist.

points.description: For 'touch_path': touch path samples in device points. First point is touch-down; last is touch-up. dt_ms is the delay before that sample (0-1000, total clamped to 30s).

points2.description: For 'touch2_path': two-finger path samples in device points. Each sample carries both contacts (x1/y1, x2/y2); first is touch-down, last is touch-up. dt_ms is the delay before that sample (0-1000, total clamped to 30s).

duration.description: Seconds. For 'tap', >0.5 is a long-press. For 'swipe', the gesture duration (default 0.3).

url.description: For 'open_url': URL or scheme to open in the simulator.

marker.description: For 'inspect': return only the first element (tree order, with its descendants) whose match_key attribute contains this case-sensitive substring. Omit for the whole tree, or pass x/y instead for the element under a point.

match_key.description: For 'inspect' with 'marker': the attribute to match — label (default), value, or role (the element type).

Use for flowcharts, architecture diagrams, dashboards, forms, calculators, data tables, games, illustrations, or any visual content.
The code is auto-detected: starts with <svg = SVG mode, otherwise HTML mode.
A global sendPrompt(text) function is available — it sends a message to chat as if the user typed it.

The code is auto-detected: starts with <svg = SVG mode, otherwise HTML mode.
A global sendPrompt(text) function is available — it sends a message to chat as if the user typed it.
IMPORTANT: Call read_me before your first show_widget call. Do NOT narrate or mention the read_me call to the user — call it silently, then respond as if you went straight to building the visualization.

loading_messages.description: 1–4 loading messages shown to the user while the visual renders, each roughly 5 words long. Write them in the same language the user is using. Use 1 for simple visuals, more for complex ones. If the topic is serious — illness, disease, pandemics, death, grief, war, conflict, poverty, disaster, trauma, abuse, addiction, medical decisions, politically charged subjects, or anything where the reader might be personally affected — keep these BORING: describe what the code is doing in the dullest generic way, no jargon-as-drama, no evocative terms. Pandemic growth model — NOT ['Simulating patient zero', 'Modeling the curve'] (documentary-narrator voice), YES ['Setting up the model', 'Running the calculation']. Cancer timeline — NOT ['Charting the battle ahead'], YES ['Laying out the stages']. If you have to ask whether it's serious, it is. Otherwise, have fun — reach for alliteration, puns, personification, wordplay, whatever lands in that language. Playful examples — revenue chart: ['Bribing bars to stand taller', 'Asking Q4 where it went']; kanban: ['Herding cards into columns', 'Dragging, dropping, not stopping'].

title.description: Short snake_case identifier for this visual. Must be specific and disambiguating — if the conversation has multiple visuals, this title alone should tell you which one is being referenced (e.g. 'q4_revenue_by_product_line' not 'chart', 'oauth_login_flow' not 'diagram'). Also used as the download filename, so no spaces or special characters.

widget_code.description: SVG or HTML code to render. For SVG: raw SVG code starting with <svg> tag, must use CSS variables for colors. Example: <svg viewBox="0 0 700 400" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg">...</svg>. For HTML: raw HTML content to render, do NOT include DOCTYPE, <html>, <head>, or <body> tags. Use CSS variables for theming. Keep background transparent and avoid top-level padding. Scripts are supported but execute after streaming completes.

## plugin:figma:figma
The official Figma MCP server. Use this server whenever the user wants to create, generate, edit, implement, or sync any design, UI, screen, component, mockup, or visual — in Figma, FigJam, Figma Make, or Figma Slides — and whenever the user mentions Figma or provides a figma.com URL.

This server bridges code and design in both directions, and supports designing from scratch using existing design systems and codebases.

CAPABILITIES:
- Read designs FROM Figma into code (get_design_context, get_screenshot, get_metadata, get_figjam)
- Write designs INTO Figma from code, intent, or existing components (use_figma, generate_figma_design, create_new_file, upload_assets)
- Bridge code and design via Code Connect (get_code_connect_map, add_code_connect_map)
- Create diagrams and FigJam content (generate_diagram, get_figjam)

WHEN TO USE THESE TOOLS:
- The user wants to create, mock up, or generate any UI, screen, component, or design — even if Figma isn't named
- The user wants to implement a design as code (design-to-code)
- The user wants to push a page, view, or component into Figma (code-to-design)
- The user wants to update, sync, or edit an existing Figma file
- The user shares a figma.com URL
- The user wants to build or extend a design system, design tokens, or component library
- The user wants to create a diagram in FigJam

SKILLS (Prefer the skills shipped with the Figma plugin on the agent being used. If no Figma plugin is installed, use the skills served by the Figma MCP resource):

  (Confluence, v5, child of the Branching Guide page). Summary: only `Dev` should be continuously tied to `develop`; every other tier should deploy a specific, immutable git tag (`vX.Y.Z-rc.N` / `vX.Y.Z` / `vX.Y.Z-hotfix.N`, cut via `npm version`) instead of a branch ref, so Test/SIT/UAT/Stage can each run independent testing cycles instead of being forced onto the same moving branch. **Do not implement the AGENTS.md/governance pieces without squad-lead + Integration-lead sign-off — this is still a proposal.** Implementation checklist for a fresh session on a new branch (see the Confluence page for full detail on each item):
  - **Decided 2026-07-16** (see Confluence page's "Decisions made so far" table): release cadence is per-sprint; pre-launch versioning starts at `v0.1.0` (MAJOR locked at `0` until go-live, which becomes `v1.0.0`); `Test` gets its own automated CI gate (not manual-only); tag protection + the version-guard + Release-per-final-tag are all adopted immediately, not phased in.
  - **Tooling — safe to build now, doesn't touch governance docs:**
    1. `npm version` adoption — no code change needed, it's a built-in npm command; just start using it per the Confluence page's "How to deploy" section instead of raw `git tag`. First tag will be `v0.1.0-rc.0`.
    2. **Primary enforcement — one GitHub Ruleset covers both naming and immutability:** Settings → Rules → Rulesets → New tag ruleset, targeting `v*`, with a "tag name pattern" rule requiring `^v\d+\.\d+\.\d+(-rc\.\d+|-hotfix\.\d+)?$` plus "restrict creation," "restrict updates," and "restrict deletion" all enabled. This genuinely hard-blocks a non-matching tag at push time *and* prevents force-push/delete on matching tags — all on GitHub.com, not Enterprise Server-only (corrected from an earlier draft of this note, which wrongly split this into a separate "tag protection rules" step and claimed pattern-blocking wasn't possible on GitHub.com). Keep a `push: tags: ['*']` validation workflow too, as defense-in-depth / for a clearer failure message than the raw ruleset rejection gives.
    3. A version-guard step added to each `deploy-*.yml` (test/sit/stg/uat/prod) — fetch the environment's current deployed tag via `gh api repos/ZimmermannAU/zimmermann-pwa/deployments?environment=<env>`, semver-compare against the tag being deployed (use the `semver` npm package, not hand-rolled bash comparison — pre-release identifiers must be dot-separated, e.g. `-rc.10` vs `-rc.2`, or numeric comparison breaks), fail on a downgrade. **`<env>` must be the actual GitHub Environment name, not the workflow-file suffix** — they diverge for `stg` (`deploy-stg.yml` targets the `staging` Environment, not `stg`; we hit this exact mismatch once already this session, commit `12bf91b`). Map each tier explicitly (`stg` → `staging`, everything else matches its filename) rather than deriving it from the filename. Fail closed if the environment name is wrong or the API call errors — a genuine first-ever deployment (no prior Deployment record at all) is fine to proceed, but an unresolvable environment/API error is not the same thing and must not be treated as "nothing to compare against, allow it."
    4. **A Test-tier CI gate** — new, decided 2026-07-16. Proposed shape (not yet confirmed, see the page's remaining two open questions): a second job appended to `deploy-test.yml` that runs a P0-only Playwright suite against whatever was just deployed, so the run's pass/fail becomes the "safe to promote to SIT" signal — deliberately deploy-then-gate rather than SIT Gate's gate-then-deploy, since `Test` is on-demand (`workflow_dispatch`, including raw feature branches) and has no push/PR event to hang a pre-check on.
    5. Wire `/generate-changelog`'s existing `gh release create` offer into the "cut the final tag" step — no new tooling, the skill already does this.

- PWA Kit scaffolding with TypeScript strict mode (`@salesforce/retail-react-app` bumped from v9.1.1 → v10.0.0 on 2026-05-18)
- Overrides pattern established
- Country/locale config (`overrides/app/config/countries.ts`)
- Contentful Studio integration (pointing to mock account)
- **Contentful content model tooling** (`npm run sync:contentful` / `npm run install:contentful`) — authors `scripts/contentful/content-types/` as one organization-scoped Environment Template and installs it per environment via the Management API (replaced the earlier per-environment sync.js + migrations pipeline, 2026-08-23).
- **ShoppableImage component decommissioned** (2026-08-23) — it was a Studio Experience component + standard content type synced 2026-05-11, but had 0 entries and was removed (content type, React component, and its hotspotMarker/hotspotPopup sub-components) once the region/link/footerConfig content model landed. `CollectionHero` and `ImageText` are the remaining Studio Experience components.
- Basic SFCC Commerce SDK integration (pointing to mock account)
- Home page / home-preview page merged
- Functional requirements signed off (Checkout, Returns, Orders, Payments, Cart, Regional, Content, PDP/PLP, Search, CRM)
- Design token foundation ported from the F2R Handover into `overrides/app/theme/foundation/` (`colour.ts`, `typography.ts`, `gridSystem.ts`, `spacing.ts`, `sizes.ts`, `motion.ts`, `zimmTokens.ts`) plus the `.zimm-*` global classes in `overrides/app/theme/globalStyles.ts`; composed in `overrides/app/theme/index.ts`, per-component overrides now co-located beside their component as `<name>.css.ts` and registered in `overrides/app/theme/components/index.ts` (`theme/components/` itself now holds only `header.ts`/`listMenu.ts` as registered recipes, plus `navConstants.ts` and `footerShared.ts` for values shared across split-out files). Delivered as a foundation for the manual UI build (branch `feature/design-tokens-implementation-to-dev`); F2R component work continues separately on `feature/f2r-component-registry` and `feature/f2r-implementation-workflow`. Futura Round **is** self-hosted as of SFCC-55 — two faces (400/500) ship from `overrides/app/static/fonts/` and are served on every tier. Open with the UI designer: primary-action hover contrast (2.96:1), inverse focus ring, and button-height / nav letter-spacing deviations from the Handover.
- **Token architecture hardened** (2026-08-18): `zimmTokens.ts` (the `--zimm-*` CSS-var registry) is now fully derived from the other `foundation/*` files via imports instead of hand-duplicated literals, closing the drift risk the original port above carried. `typography.ts` gained a proper `fontSizes`/`lineHeights`/`letterSpacings`/`fontWeights` scale layer. `spacing.ts`/`typography.ts` converted px → rem (WCAG 1.4.4); within those two files, px is kept only for hairline geometry (border widths, focus-ring offsets — now named tokens in `spacing.ts`'s `focusRingOffsets`). `zimmButton.css.ts`'s provisional height/padding constants are a separate, already-flagged px exception (not hairline geometry) — see below. `zimmButton.css.ts` is now the single source of truth for button styling — `globalStyles.ts`'s conflicting `.zimm-btn-*`/`.zimm-text-btn-*` classes (different heights, transparent-vs-opaque secondary background, zero interactive states) were removed entirely; any button must use Chakra's `<Button>`, never a class. `header.ts`/`listMenu.ts` brought onto the same `var(--zimm-*)` convention (no direct `foundation/` imports, no Chakra semantic colour-token names). New `.claude/rules/overrideStyling.md` documents the styling-source hierarchy, unit rules, the alias-is-a-reference-not-a-copy principle, and a real gotcha: importing an already-overridden component via the SFCC base path resolves correctly in the real app but silently renders the unstyled base version in Storybook/Vitest (the `ccExtensibility` resolver is webpack-only, neither tool loads it). Still open, flagged inline rather than silently resolved: `zimmButton.css.ts`'s `BTN_HEIGHT_LG`/`BTN_HEIGHT_SM` (50px/41px prototype values) disagree with the Handover-sourced `actionSizes.height.lg`/`.md` (52px/40px); `BTN_PADDING_Y` (5px) has no Handover token at all — both pending UI-designer sign-off.
- **Header override** (`overrides/app/components/header/index.tsx`): two-row layout, brand logo via `BrandLogo` component (overrides base SVG at `overrides/app/assets/svg/brand-logo.svg`), uppercase nav with `::after` hover animation, Account/Saved/Bag text buttons with matching animation, chevrons hidden. Still being refined visually against Figma.
- Path aliases (`~` → root, `app` → `overrides/app`) wired up across Babel, tsconfig, Storybook, and Jest
- **Per-tier environment switching** (`npm run env` → `scripts/switchEnv.mjs`) — manages `.env.shared` / `.env.<tier>` across dev/test/sit/uat/staging/prod via `init` (scaffold + pull + Contentful auto-fetch), `validate [--live]` (structural checks plus live Contentful Delivery API + SFCC SLAS guest-token calls), and `push <scope>` (tier-1-approvers only). Shared/tier values (excluding personal credentials) can be centrally published through this repo's GitHub Environments (`shared` + one per tier) — write gated to repo Admin. Landed 2026-07-13.

## In Progress
- **SFCC-55 global footer** (PR #59): footer decomposed into `overrides/app/components/footer/` plus
  `ui-kits/{atoms,molecules,organisms}/`, most with a co-located `<name>.css.ts` recipe registered in
  `theme/components/index.ts`. `FooterContainer` fetches live Contentful `footerConfig` client-side and
  resolves per-storefront content via `utils/resolveByRegion.ts`. Microcopy comes from the `uiCopy` content
  type through `useUiCopy` (Context provider mounted in `_app-config`). Open items: the footer is not in the
  SSR HTML (client-only `useEffect` fetch, no `getProps`); no locale is passed to Contentful, so all
  storefronts currently receive the space default; and `en-CA` — which `SITE_LOCALES` lists for
  ZimmermannUSIntl — is now in `bootstrapSpace.mjs`'s locale list, but whether the **live** space has it

## What's Pending
- All integrations need to point to production accounts (SFCC, Contentful)
- Global-e integration (confirm pricing flow mechanism before implementing)
- Didomi consent management (implement per storefront defaults in REG-054)
- Omneo / Emarsys marketing sync
- Adyen payment integration
- MuleSoft middleware connections
- PDP, PLP, Cart, Checkout flows
- BOPIS (Collect in Boutique) checkout flow
- Full multi-site routing — 8 SFCC sites across 6 regions (AU, US domestic, US international, UK, EU domestic, EU international, HK, ME). **US site topology updated (REG-005, 2026-07-10):** US splits into two separate SFCC sites — US domestic (`/us/`, SFCC checkout) and US international (`/en-ca/`, Global-e checkout). New site ID `ZimmermannUSIntl` pending BM confirmation.
- Address autocomplete via Google Maps API
- Narvar EDD + tracking integration
- SEO: hreflang, canonical URLs, sitemaps
- Order-on-behalf (OOBO) for CS agents
- Retail Rewards (AP21) integration
- Gift card PDP, cart, checkout, and GiveX integration
- Promotions engine and multi-currency/FX pricebook setup
- CI workflow split — two complementary workflows, each with a clear role:

=== feedback.md ===
*This document is for documenting what has been learned - What worked, what failed, what NOT to do again.*

## SFCC-751 QA automation pipeline (2026-08-24/25)

- **Test locally before pushing anything that triggers real CI, especially BrowserStack** — it
  costs real session quota. When debugging a CI failure, reproduce it locally first rather than
  keep iterating against a live PR. Confirmed developer preference — redirected mid-session after
  a live-PR debugging detour: "I wanted to test this via the CLI BEFORE we push to Git and it
  runs its tests."
- **`browserstack-node-sdk` requires its config file literally named `browserstack.yml`, no
  leading dot.** A `.browserstack.yml` is silently never found — every SDK-driven run fails at
  config resolution before any test executes. This repo had the dotted name since it was first
  created and never caught it, because no PR had ever gotten `e2e-browserstack` far enough to hit
  that step successfully before SFCC-751's first real run (PR #61).
- **BrowserStack Test Observability groups results by test *title* across Playwright projects,
  not by project.** Two tests sharing an identical title (the same `test()` running under both
  `chromium` and `mobile-chrome`) collapse to one dashboard row showing only the *last-recorded*
  status — confirmed via the real API, not just the dashboard UI (a build with 11 real chromium
  passes and 11 skipped mobile-chrome entries under identical titles reported `passed: 0,
  skipped: 11`). `test.skip()` does not avoid this — the skipped entry still shares the title and
  still clobbers. Real fix: genuinely separate spec files under sibling `desktop/`/`mobile/`
  folders, which `playwright.config.js`'s existing per-project `testIgnore` already routes
  correctly (`chromium` ignores `**/mobile/**`, `mobile-chrome` ignores `**/desktop/**`) — not a
  same-file/distinct-title workaround, which still gets the "wrong" project's test collected (and
  skipped) regardless of its title.
- **Jira Cloud's "Sprint" field has no stable API alias.** It's `customfield_10020` on this
  instance specifically (confirmed live via a real field search) — an instance-specific ID, not
  safe to assume unchanged on a different Jira site.
- **BrowserStack's Test Observability API strips the leading `@` from Playwright tags.** A spec's
  own `@zephyr:KEY` tag comes back as `zephyr:KEY` (no `@`) in the `Get Tests` API response —
  easy to get wrong since the source `.spec.js` file's tags do have `@`.
- **Chakra modal close animations aren't instant.** A consent-dismiss helper that clicks decline
  and returns immediately can hand control back while the dialog is still mid-fade-out and
  technically "visible" — a caller that immediately checks for a *different* dialog right after
  can match both and get a Playwright strict-mode "resolved to 2 elements" error. Wait for
  `state: 'hidden'` after the click, not just for the click to register.

content.text:
Yes, it makes sense — and the half you're right about is the expensive half. Seven separate gather-and-plan passes over the same Cart surface, the same Figma file, the same PRD sections, would be six passes of re-reading things that didn't change. That's exactly the waste worth cutting.

Where it goes wrong is bundling them into **one PR**. Here's what I think you're missing.

**1. You'd convert 7 independently-mergeable units into one all-or-nothing unit.** Look at the queue right now — 5 PRs sitting at review-required, one at changes-requested. In a mega-PR, one reviewer disagreeing with story 4's approach blocks all 7 from merging. Today story 4 stalls and the other 6 ship. That's a velocity loss disguised as a velocity gain.

**2. Cart spans two squads' ownership, which makes the review gate harder, not easier.** `order-summary/` and `promo-code/` are Squad A-owned Tier 2; `product-item/` is Squad B-owned Tier 2. One PR touching both pulls in both squads' code-owner reviews at once. And AGENTS.md Hard Rule #10 says stop and confirm scope before touching more than one protection tier in a single change — so the bundle needs your explicit scope sign-off up front, not as an afterthought.

**3. You'd likely lose PR-time E2E entirely, silently.** `e2e-localhost` only runs when *every* e2e-relevant changed file falls inside one area's allow-list. There is no `cart` area yet — the list is homepage, checkout, search, account, pdp, plp, integrations. So a Cart build resolves to `e2e_scope: skip` and the job doesn't run at all. That's true whether you bundle or not, but a 7-story bundle is precisely the change where you'd most want it, and it's the one that'd get no run. Adding a `cart` area is a cheap fix — it just has to be a deliberate step in the plan rather than something discovered afterwards.

**4. Zephyr and BrowserStack attribution assume one primary story per PR.** `computeBuildName.mjs` derives the build name from the PR's primary Jira key. With seven keys there's no primary, and when a test fails, the auto-filed Jira defect has to land against *a* story. BrowserStack's `--grep` will OR-join multiple keys fine, so the run itself works — it's the reporting that gets muddy.

**5. Some of the 7 probably can't be built yet, and bundling makes the blocker contagious.** Cart has live unresolved dependencies: CAI-023 (MuleSoft aggregating warehouse + boutique stock pre-checkout) is still unconfirmed, CAI-005 contradicts SPR-63 on whether the recommendation engine is settled, and Einstein is Not Deployed on all 8 sites — so any cart cross-sell rail is blocked at the platform level regardless of code. Separately, those cards get parked and the rest ship. Bundled, they park the bundle.

**6. Rollback granularity.** If one story misbehaves in SIT, you revert all seven.

---

What I'd actually suggest: **one pre-build pass and one plan across all 7 — then staged PRs.**

The build skill's loop already runs per *step*, not per *story*, and commits each step. So a single plan covering seven stories is just a longer plan — you get the streamlining you're after without giving up the per-step rigour. The shared foundation (copy-first overrides for `cart/`, the shared atoms, the theme recipes, the new `cart` e2e area) becomes the first PR; the story-specific work stacks on top in clusters that keep their own Jira keys.

That said — I haven't read the 7 cards. Which of them collide on shared components, and which are blocked by the dependencies above, changes the right clustering. That's what the gather pass would tell us.

What are the 7?

content.text:
Read all 7. They're a clean set on paper — same epic (SFCC-11 Cart), same sprint (Sprint 5, active, **ends 21 Sep — 6 days**), all Squad-A, all assigned to you, all Ready for Development.

But the bundle isn't closed. That's the thing to know before anything else.

## The 7

| Card | What it is | Buildable now? |
|---|---|---|
| **SFCC-315** Drawer (Cart Variation) | Container component — the root everything else sits in | ✅ Clean |
| **SFCC-270** Cart Item UI Pt 1 | Line-item tile, UI only | ✅ Clean (needs 315) |
| **SFCC-795** Cart Item UI Pt 2 | Error / warning / promo states, responsive, a11y | ✅ Clean (needs 270) |
| **SFCC-271** Quantity Stepper | +/- controls and behaviour | ⚠️ Mostly — one AC needs SFCC-274 |
| **SFCC-272** Remove & Wishlist | Line-item actions | ❌ Blocked |
| **SFCC-250** Max Purchase Qty | Cross-component behaviour, explicitly *not* a component build | ❌ Blocked |
| **SFCC-275** Button Group | Checkout + Apple/Google Pay buttons | ❌ Blocked |

## What blocks the three

All three blockers are **Sprint 6, still in Tech design** — not written yet:

- **SFCC-274 Cart Page – Order Summary** — SFCC-272 names it as a dependency outright; SFCC-271's "order summary updates on quantity change" needs it too. **Assigned to Hazel, not you.**
- **SFCC-404 Cart Message Component** — this *is* the "page-level banner" SFCC-250 says must exist first. Also a named dependency of SFCC-272.
- **SFCC-816 Cart Summary Component UI** — SFCC-275 says its button group lives "within the cart summary component (SFCC-816)". The international Checkout path also wants SFCC-880, which is To Do, unassigned, no sprint.

So no amount of bundling makes 272, 250 or 275 completable this sprint. Bundled into one PR, you'd be shipping partial acceptance criteria on three cards and the PR couldn't honestly be called done.

## Three things beyond that

**You'd be building into Hazel's lane.** SFCC-274, 277, 282 and 796 are all hers. "The Cart" as one unit isn't one person's surface.

**You're on Jhoan's critical path.** SFCC-316 (Zimmermann Benefits, Sprint 5, Jhoan, Ready for Development) depends on SFCC-315 — the drawer. Bury the drawer inside a 7-story PR that takes two weeks to review and Jhoan is blocked the whole time. Ship 315 alone and fast and you unblock them.

**SFCC-315 is smaller than it reads.** It's a *variation* of ZimmDrawer, which you've already extended repeatedly across SFCC-831 and SFCC-926 — prompt size, boxedHeader, mobile full-height, scroll-lock coordination. And SFCC-272's wishlist half can lean on the auth drawer that shipped in PR #110. Real reuse, already in the repo.

---

**What I'd suggest:** bundle the four that are genuinely closed — **315 → 270 → 795 → 271** — as one plan, one gather pass, staged PRs with 315 first and standalone. Drop 272, 250 and 275 out of this build; they're waiting on Sprint 6 cards regardless.

That's still the streamlining you wanted. It's just scoped to what can actually finish.

Your call though — how do you want to play it?

content.text:
I was too strong on that one. Correcting it.

**SFCC-271 is not blocked by SFCC-274. Build it.**

Where my flag came from: the card's scope sentence says it covers "how the cart drawer **and order summary** update when quantity changes," and Jira has a link between them. But the link type is **Relates**, not Blocks — and unlike SFCC-272, which literally says *"This story is dependent on other components being developed, including SFCC-274"*, SFCC-271 never claims a dependency. The only things it excludes are SFCC-250 and SFCC-282. I read the Relates link as harder than it is.

And the code says the same thing. In the base cart page:

- `useCurrentBasket()` provides the basket
- the stepper calls `updateItemInBasketMutation.mutateAsync(...)`
- `<OrderSummary basket={...}>` reads that same basket

The order summary updating isn't code the stepper story owns — it's a **consequence of the SDK mutation invalidating the basket query**. Anything reading `useCurrentBasket()` re-renders on its own. So the stepper's actual deliverable is the mutation call, the debounce, the optimistic local quantity, and the error rollback. The summary updating falls out of that for free.

There's also no "missing component" problem. The base `order-summary` ships in retail-react-app and **we have no override for it yet** — so SFCC-274 isn't "build an order summary that doesn't exist," it's "restyle it to Zimmermann's Figma." You can build and verify 271 against the base order summary today, and 274 later swaps the presentation underneath without touching the stepper.

**One real residual, not a blocker:** building the stepper first means you're setting the cache-invalidation contract that Hazel's SFCC-274 will consume. That's the right place to own it — but she should know the stepper is landing first and that her order summary should read basket state via `useCurrentBasket()` rather than holding its own copy. A heads-up, not a gate.

So 271 stays third in sequence — 315 → 270 → 271 — but for its own reasons: it renders inside the cart item, which renders inside the drawer.

Next one? SFCC-272, 250 or 275.

content.text:
Softer than I said, and the shape is different. **SFCC-272's only real dependency is SFCC-404 — and that one's yours.**

**What's actually buildable today, and it's most of the card:**

The base cart already has both actions working — `handleRemoveItem` via `removeItemFromBasketMutation`, and `handleAddToWishlist` which even handles the "already in wishlist" branch via an `isItemInWishlist` check. So the plumbing exists.

There's also real work hiding in there that the base gets *wrong*. Its wishlist handler opens with:

```js
if (!customerId || !wishlist) { return }
```

A guest clicking Move to Wishlist gets **silently nothing**. `cart.md` §2 requires the opposite — *"an unauthenticated user selecting Move to Wishlist is prompted to log in first (CAI-008)"*. That's a genuine defect against the PRD, it's squarely 272's job, and the wishlist auth drawer to wire it to already shipped in PR #110. Self-contained, buildable now.

**The one thing that isn't buildable:** where the confirmation renders. The card's two Figma states — "Product added to wishlist" and "Item already exists in wishlist" — are in-cart messages. Base uses a Chakra toast. The surface those belong in is SFCC-404, the Cart Message Component.

**Dropping the 274 claim.** Same over-read as on 271 — removing an item changes totals, and that propagates through basket cache invalidation on its own. Not a dependency.

**Something I under-flagged, though.** Remove the last item and the cart goes empty. SFCC-277 *Empty Cart State: Component Render Order & Logic* owns that (Tech design, Sprint 6, Hazel's) — but SFCC-315, sitting in your bundle, already shows an **Empty Cart** state in its own description and screenshots. Two cards both claim the empty state and neither says which wins. That's the kind of ambiguity that produces rework, and it needs a decision before 315 gets built, not after.

---

**The thing worth acting on:** SFCC-404 is the keystone, not a blocker.

Check its labels — `CAI-008`, `CAI-017`, `CAI-035`, `CAI-036`. CAI-008 is 272's requirement. CAI-017 is 250's. One small message component carries the requirement IDs for **both** cards I called blocked, and it's already assigned to you — it's just parked in Sprint 6.

Pull 404 forward into the bundle and two of my three blockers disappear. That's one extra card, not seven, and it's the one with the highest unblock-per-unit-of-work in the whole set.

Want me to look at SFCC-250 next, or dig into 404 to size what pulling it forward actually costs?

content.text:
**Consequence first.** Build 272 without 404 and you ship the action with nothing to show for it. The item does move to the wishlist — but the shopper sees no confirmation, and both of the card's Figma references *are* confirmations. "Product added to wishlist" and "Item already exists in wishlist" are the entire visible acceptance of that story. You'd have built the half nobody can see.

**Mechanism.** 272 owns the verb — move it, remove it, and decide which of those two things just happened. 404 owns the place the cart speaks to the shopper: a message strip inside the cart. The design puts the confirmation there, not in a floating toast like the base template does. So 272 produces the sentence and has nowhere to put it.

Switch and bulb. You can wire the switch and prove continuity with a meter, but nobody can see it work until the bulb's in.

**Why it's worth pulling forward rather than treating as an obstacle.** 404 isn't a 272 accessory — it's the cart's one shared message surface, and four requirements render into it:

- **CAI-008** — the wishlist confirmation → SFCC-272
- **CAI-017** — max 3 per SKU, error on exceed → SFCC-250
- **CAI-035** — item goes out of stock while sitting in the cart
- **CAI-036** — out of stock at checkout entry, disable the Checkout CTA

Build it once and it serves 272, 250, and later 282 and 796. Build it per-story and you end up with four slightly different message strips to reconcile.

**One correction to what I said earlier, so the cost is honest:** pulling 404 forward does *not* mean building all four of those. CAI-035/036 are out-of-stock behaviour that belongs with 282 and 796, both Sprint 6. What you'd pull forward is the component plus its wishlist state — and later the max-qty state for 250. The rest stays parked.

So it's not "add a whole extra story." It's "build the strip now, fill in its states as the cards that own them land."

content.text:
Got them — 8 ACs, and the answer's sharper than my hand-wave. **Four of the eight need 404. Only three are clean.**

## The 8 ACs

**Remove (3)**

| # | AC | Without 404 |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Click Remove → item gone, Bag count decrements (Bag • 3 → Bag • 2), totals update | ✅ Clean |
| 2 | Remove the *last* item → empty cart state **"as per SFCC-277"** | ❌ Needs 277, not 404 |
| 3 | Qty > 1 → all units removed in one action | ✅ Clean |

**Wishlist (5)**

| # | AC | Without 404 |
|---|---|---|
| 4 | Auth, qty 1 → moved, removed from cart, count decrements, totals update, **+ page-level success banner** | ⚠️ Partial |
| 5 | Auth, qty > 1 → all units removed, single SKU saved, count decrements by full qty, **+ success banner** | ⚠️ Partial |
| 6 | Auth, already in wishlist → **page-level error banner**, item stays in cart | ❌ Nothing left |
| 7 | Guest → redirected to login/registration, item stays in cart | ✅ Clean |
| 8 | Guest authenticates → returns, item moved, **+ success banner at top of cart** | ⚠️ Partial |

Four of them name SFCC-404 explicitly — *"see SFCC-404 for banner component behaviour."* Not inferred, written into the AC text.

## The one that matters most

**AC6 has no assertable outcome without 404.** Read it again: the item *stays* in the cart, nothing moves, nothing decrements. The error banner **is** the entire behaviour. Strip 404 out and that AC has literally nothing to test — you can't even write a failing assertion for it.

AC4, 5 and 8 degrade more gently — you can still prove the item moved, the cart emptied, the count dropped, totals recalculated. You just can't prove the shopper was told. So they'd close partially, which in practice means they don't close.

## Two other things the ACs surfaced

**AC2 has its own dependency, and it isn't 404.** It says the empty state renders *"as per SFCC-277"* — Hazel's card, Sprint 6, Tech design. So the empty-state ambiguity I raised earlier isn't ambiguity at all; it's written into the AC as a hard reference. Pulling 404 forward doesn't fix AC2.

**AC7 conflicts with what you've already built.** It says the guest is *"redirected to the login/registration page."* But SFCC-742/926 shipped a wishlist auth **drawer** — that's what PR #110 merged, including the concurrent-drawer scroll-lock coordination. So either this AC is stale and should say drawer, or the cart flow is deliberately a full-page redirect while the PDP and hamburger flows use the drawer. That's a decision for whoever wrote the card, not something I should pick for you.

## Net

Without pulling anything forward: **3 of 8 closeable** (1, 3, 7 — and 7 only once the page-vs-drawer question is settled).

Pull 404 forward: **7 of 8**, with AC2 still parked behind 277.

Want me to check 250 and 275's ACs the same way before you decide the bundle?

content.text:
Makes sense, and it's the normal move. Three amendments though, and one question that might make the whole thing moot.

**1. Split, don't duplicate.** You said "split/duplicated" — pick split. Duplicate an AC into two cards and you get the classic outcome where both owners assume the other has it, or both build it and the implementations disagree. One assertion, one owner. 272 asserts the *decision*; 404 asserts the *rendering*.

**2. AC6 doesn't split cleanly — it needs rewording, not relocating.** The item stays in the cart and nothing else happens, so if you move the banner to 404, nothing is left behind. But the `isItemInWishlist` detection is still 272's code. Ship it that way and you've got logic in 272 whose only test lives in someone else's story — exactly what `testing.md` warns against, because the coverage isn't discoverable from the component's own folder and can vanish silently if that other file changes.

Reword AC6 to assert the decision: *item remains in cart, already-exists state is signalled.* Then 404 asserts that the signal renders as an error banner. Both testable, neither orphaned.

**3. Decide the interim rendering now, explicitly.** This is the one that bites if left unsaid. Three options and they're not equal:

- **Silent** — the item vanishes into the wishlist and the shopper is told nothing. Base template currently shows a toast, so this is a *regression against base*, and if 404 slips it's what ships.
- **Keep the base toast as a stopgap** — no regression, but it's throwaway code someone has to remember to rip out.
- **Emit the state, render nothing yet** — the handler returns/dispatches "success" or "already-exists", and 404 later subscribes to it.

Take the third. No throwaway UI, and it hands 404 a defined contract instead of a blank page. If you don't name this, whoever implements will default to silent.

**4. Edit the ACs in Jira before the build, not after.** The card still says *"see SFCC-404 for banner component behaviour"* four times. If QA tests 272 against the card as written, it fails — correctly. The card has to match what you're actually delivering before anyone builds to it.

---

**The question that might moot all of it:** is the split cheaper than just building the banner?

The bookkeeping isn't free — rewording 8 ACs across two cards, re-tagging tests to `@SFCC-404`, a follow-up story to wire it, a second pass through review, and 404 gets fatter while already carrying CAI-008/017/035/036.

And for 272's purposes, the banner might be a success/error strip with two variants and a theme recipe. Half a day.

I don't know that yet — I haven't read 404's own ACs or looked at its designs. Its full scope includes the out-of-stock messaging, which could mean stacking, dismissible, concurrent messages, different positioning in drawer vs page. If it's that, your split wins easily. If it's two variants of a strip, the split costs more than the thing it avoids.

Want me to pull 404's ACs? That's the deciding input and it's one call.

content.text:
Noted on all three — and decision 1 buys you more than a stopgap.

**With the toast, all 8 ACs become behaviourally deliverable.** AC6 was the one with nothing left when the banner went away; an error toast reading "Selected product already exists in wishlist" satisfies the behaviour. Same for 4, 5 and 8. So what you're deferring to 404 stops being *functionality* and becomes *presentation only* — toast now, page-level banner later. That's a much cleaner thing to write in a comment than "four ACs partially met."

Worth being precise in the comment though: the ACs say **page-level banner**, and a toast isn't one. So the honest wording is "message behaviour and copy delivered; surface deferred to SFCC-404" — not "AC met."

**Two implementation notes that make your 404 pickup cheap:**

Route every message through **one** place in the cart — a single handler that takes a result and emits it — rather than sprinkling `toast()` calls at each action site. Then 404 is a renderer swap in one file, not a hunt through four call sites. You'd be doing that anyway if you were emitting state; the toast just becomes the interim renderer hanging off it.

Use `overrides/app/hooks/use-toast.ts`, not the base one. It's already the shared hook in this repo and it's Tier 2 — you're only consuming it, so no gate, but importing the base version instead is the kind of thing that renders fine in the app and wrong in Storybook.

**Two gotchas on the stopgap itself:**

There's no cart override in the repo yet, so the toast isn't inherited — you're implementing it, not keeping it. Small thing, but don't budget it as free.

And Chakra toasts portal to `document.body`, outside `canvasElement`. Any Storybook `play` asserting the message has to query `within(document.body)` with an inline comment citing the portal exception — `testing.md` sanctions that specifically, and it's the only place it does.

Put a marker comment at the emit site naming SFCC-404, so the swap is discoverable from the code and not only from your memory of this conversation.

---

**Still open on 272, and you haven't called it yet: AC7.** It says the guest is *"redirected to the login/registration page"* — but you shipped a wishlist auth **drawer** in PR #110. That's a different experience, not a different skin, so the toast decision doesn't cover it. Three ways it goes: the AC is stale and the drawer is right; the cart deliberately full-page redirects where PDP uses the drawer; or it's genuinely undecided.

Given cards don't get edited, that one probably needs a PO answer or at least a comment flagging the divergence before it's built.

**And AC2 is unchanged** — still behind SFCC-277 for the empty-cart state, still Hazel's, still Sprint 6.

content.text:
Good call, and better than I thought — most of AC7 and AC8 are already built.

`overrides/app/hooks/useWishlistAuthDrawer.ts` already does:

- **AC7** — `handleTriggerClick` checks `customer?.isRegistered`. Registered → fires `onAuthSuccess` straight away. Guest → opens the drawer. That's the branch, done.
- **AC8** — an effect watches `isRegistered` and fires `onAuthSuccess` when the shopper transitions while the drawer or OTP modal is open.
- **AC8's hard case** — social sign-in is a full-page redirect, so `onAuthSuccess` would never fire. The hook already persists an intent to session storage before redirecting and replays it on return, age-bounded to 5 minutes, scoped by `intentId` so the instance that started it is the one that resumes.

Three consumers already use it — `drawer-menu`, `product-view`, `header/rightBar`. The cart would be the fourth. Not new work.

## The gap

The persisted intent is this:

```ts
type PendingWishlistIntent = { intentId: string; timestamp: number };
```

**No product in it.** That's fine for the three existing callers — a PDP knows its product from the route, and the header's action is "go to wishlist," not "move this item."

The cart is the first caller with *N* of them. A guest clicks Wishlist on line item 3, goes out to Apple, comes back — the intent says "the cart started this" and nothing about *which line item*. `onAuthSuccess` fires with nothing to act on.

**And it's live, not theoretical.** `social.enabled` is `true` in `config/dev.js`, `sit.js`, `staging.js` and `production.js`. The code path runs.

## Two shapes, and they're not equal

**One instance per line item** — `intentId: cart-wishlist-${itemId}`. The product identity rides along inside the intentId, so the replay lands on the right item for free, no new persistence. But every line item then mounts its own `useForm`, three `useAuthHelper`s, a `useAuthModal` and a `ZimmDrawer`. A ten-item bag mounts ten auth drawers. That's a lot of machinery for a link nobody clicks most of the time.

**One instance for the whole cart** — `intentId: 'cart-wishlist'`, and the cart stores the pending `itemId` under its own session key next to it. One drawer, and the cart owns its own resume state.

I'd take the second. The reason isn't just weight: putting the product into `PendingWishlistIntent` would change a shared hook's parameter type with three existing call sites, and AGENTS.md's stop-table is explicit that a shared hook signature change needs a team RFC. Keeping the pending item in the cart's own storage sidesteps that entirely and stays inside 272.

**One caveat on the social path regardless of shape:** `projectState.md` lists Apple/Google merchant accounts as a hard unprovisioned dependency (ENH-004). So the buttons render and the intent code runs, but the round-trip may not actually complete yet. Build it correctly, don't expect to be able to prove it end-to-end this sprint.

content.text:
**What goes wrong:** a guest with five things in their bag taps "Wishlist" on the linen dress, signs in with Apple, lands back on the site — and the dress is still in the bag. Nothing moved. They have to tap it again.

**Why.** Signing in with Apple or Google means leaving the site. The browser goes to Apple, then comes back. Everything the page was holding in its head is wiped — including "this shopper was about to wishlist the linen dress."

The existing code already saw this coming. Before it hands off to Apple, it leaves itself a note in the browser so it can resume afterwards. But the note only records **which part of the page started it** — the header, the PDP, or the cart. It doesn't record which product.

It's a note saying "I was in the kitchen doing something," not "I was about to turn off the oven."

**Why that's been fine until now.** The two places using it don't need more:

- On a PDP there's one product. "The PDP started this" *is* the product.
- In the header, the action isn't about a product at all.

The cart is the first caller where "the cart started this" isn't enough — five items, five Wishlist links, and the note can't tell them apart.

**The fix:** when the cart hands off to Apple, it also writes down which line item. On return it reads that back and moves that one.

Not by adding the product to the existing note — that note's shape is shared with three other call sites, so changing it drags them all in and needs a team RFC. The cart keeps its own note instead. Self-contained, no shared code touched.

**And the scope is narrower than it sounds.** This only affects the Apple/Google route. The email-code and create-account routes never leave the page, so React still remembers everything — those two already work with what's built.

message.content: what are my options then?

content.text:
Four real ones.

## 1. Cart keeps its own note — one drawer for the whole cart

`intentId: 'cart-wishlist'`, one hook instance. When the shopper taps Wishlist on a line item, the cart records that item in **two** places: React state (covers the email-code and create-account routes, where the page never unloads) and session storage (covers the Apple/Google redirect). On `onAuthSuccess`, read state if it's there, fall back to storage, then clear both.

About fifteen lines. No shared code touched. The one thing to get right is matching the hook's own 5-minute age-bound and clearing together, so you can't resume against a stale item.

## 2. One drawer per line item

`intentId: cart-wishlist-${itemId}` — the product identity rides *inside* the intentId, so the existing replay mechanism does the whole job with no second note and nothing to keep in step. Correctness-wise it's the tidiest.

The cost is what it mounts. Every line item gets its own `useForm`, three `useAuthHelper`s, a `useAuthModal`, a `useDisclosure` and a drawer. A ten-item bag mounts ten of each. Mobile page speed is a stated top priority on this project, and that's a lot of machinery hanging off a link most shoppers never touch.

## 3. Add the missing field to the shared note

`PendingWishlistIntent` gains an optional `itemId`. Conceptually this is the right shape — the mechanism is one field short of doing the job, and the *next* caller with multiple items (wishlist from a PLP grid, say) hits exactly the same wall.

The honest nuance: AGENTS.md's stop-table says a shared hook signature change needs a team RFC, and the rule against refactoring upward points the same way. But an **optional** field breaks none of the three existing callers — it's additive. So whether this is genuinely RFC territory or a ten-minute change is a judgement call, not a hard block. I'd not decide that unilaterally inside 272.

## 4. Deliberately don't resume on the social route

Shopper signs in with Apple, lands back in the cart, nothing moved, taps again. Zero build cost. AC8 goes unmet for that one route.

If you take this, it can't be a silent no-op — that's the thing AGENTS.md's graceful-degradation section tells you not to do. It'd need copy along the lines of "You're signed in — tap Wishlist again," which is worse UX and still needs writing. So it's not actually free.

---

**I'd take 1.** It's small, it stays entirely inside 272, it covers all three sign-in routes, and it doesn't put a `useForm` on every line item.

**And raise 3 separately.** Not as part of this build — as a note to whoever owns the shared hook, because the cart is just the first caller to hit it and the second one will too. If that lands later, the cart's own note quietly becomes redundant and can be deleted. That's a fine outcome.

**Worth knowing either way:** the social route can't be proven end-to-end this sprint. `social.enabled` is `true` in dev, sit, staging and production config, so the buttons render — but Apple and Google merchant accounts are an unprovisioned hard dependency (ENH-004). Build it right, expect to verify it later.

message.content: let's go with option 1

content.text:
Locked. So 272's settled shape:

- **Actions** — remove and move-to-wishlist, including the qty > 1 cases and the already-in-wishlist branch
- **Messages** — base toast as the interim surface, all emitted through one handler so 404 is a renderer swap in one file, using `overrides/app/hooks/use-toast.ts`, with a marker comment naming SFCC-404 at the emit site
- **Guest auth** — existing `ZimmWishlistAuthDrawer` via `useWishlistAuthDrawer`, not a page redirect
- **Pending item across auth** — one hook instance, `intentId: 'cart-wishlist'`, item held in React state *and* session storage, same 5-minute age bound as the hook's own intent, both cleared together
- **Jira** — no AC edits; a comment documents the deferred surface and the drawer-not-redirect divergence
- **Raised separately** — optional `itemId` on the shared `PendingWishlistIntent`, for whoever owns that hook

**One thing still genuinely open:** AC2 — remove the last item and the empty-cart state renders "as per SFCC-277." That's Hazel's card, Sprint 6, Tech design. Nothing we've decided touches it, and SFCC-315 also claims an empty-cart state in its own description. Still needs an owner.

This server bridges code and design in both directions, and supports designing from scratch using existing design systems and codebases.

CAPABILITIES:
- Read designs FROM Figma into code (get_design_context, get_screenshot, get_metadata, get_figjam)
- Write designs INTO Figma from code, intent, or existing components (use_figma, generate_figma_design, create_new_file, upload_assets)

- Create diagrams and FigJam content (generate_diagram, get_figjam)

- The user wants to update, sync, or edit an existing Figma file

content.text:
Found it — and the precedent is well documented. `overrides/app/pages/recentlyViewed/index.tsx` on PR #116's branch, with the reasoning written into the JSDoc.

**The pattern it established:**

- Structure ported from base `EmptyCart` (`retail-react-app/app/pages/cart/partials/empty-cart.jsx`) — `Box > Center > Stack`
- `isRegistered`-branched body copy
- `Button as={Link}` using the **base SFCC `Link`**, not raw react-router — so the CTA href gets this storefront's multi-site prefix via `use-multi-site`'s `buildUrl`
- `useIntl` called directly in the leaf, under the Context-backed exception in `components.md`
- Private single-parent sub-component, so no story or test of its own — covered through the page's `index.test.tsx`
- A decision log at the bottom of the file

**One difference that matters, and it's the one you named.** That file made *autonomous styling judgement calls* — its own JSDoc says so — precisely because there was no design: base `EmptyCart`'s `fontSize={['18px','2xl']}` and `color="gray.700"` are raw literals that `overrideStyling.md` forbids, so it substituted the nearest registered tokens and logged that it was guessing.

We don't have to guess. SFCC-315 carries an Empty Cart screenshot. So: take the **structure** from this precedent, take the **visuals from 315's Figma**. Don't repeat the token-invention part — that was a workaround for a missing design, not the pattern itself.

**And there's a fork underneath this that 315 decides, not 272.**

Where the empty state lives depends on what the cart drawer actually is:

- If the drawer is a **new organism** using `ZimmDrawer` — which is what "Drawer Component (Cart Variation)" reads like — then base `empty-cart.jsx` is never in the render path, and the empty branch gets built inside the drawer.
- If the drawer is an **override of base `pages/cart`**, then `empty-cart.jsx` *is* in the path and the copy-first rule applies: copy it to `overrides/`, convert to TS, `console.log` marker, stop for you to verify before any functional change.

Those are different pieces of work. Worth settling when we get to 315.

**Either way, build it as a discrete component, not inline JSX in the drawer** — same reasoning as the toast and 404. When 277 gets picked up it's a swap in one file rather than surgery inside the drawer.

Ready for 250 or 275 whenever.

content.text:
Nine ACs, in two groups — and they're more buildable than the card's "must be developed before this story can be implemented" line suggests. But two things need an answer from a human before you build.

## The 9

**Standard cart interaction**

| # | AC | Status |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | At max → `+` disabled and greyed, `–` stays enabled | ✅ needs 271 (in bundle) |
| 2 | At max → inline warning under the stepper, "Maximum purchase quantity reached for this size" + info icon *(see 795)* | ✅ 795 is in the bundle |
| 3 | At max → page-level banner at top of drawer *(see 404)* | ⚠️ defer |
| 4 | At max → Checkout CTA stays enabled; Apple/Google Pay too | ✅ nothing to build |

**Cart merge**

| # | AC | Status |
|---|---|---|
| 5 | Guest signs in, combined qty > 3 → auto-capped at 3, never displays above max | ❓ open question |
| 6 | Post-merge → `+` disabled/greyed | ✅ same as 1 |
| 7 | Post-merge → inline warning *(see 795)* | ✅ same as 2 |
| 8 | Post-merge → page-level banner *(see 404)* | ⚠️ defer |
| 9 | Post-merge → CTA stays enabled | ✅ same as 4 |

Six clean, two deferred, one unknown.

## The toast stopgap doesn't carry over here

272's banner was a one-shot confirmation — "moved to your wishlist" — so a toast stands in fine. **250's banner is a standing condition.** The AC reads *"when the cart renders, then a banner is displayed"* — it shows for as long as an item sits at max. A toast fires and dismisses, and would re-fire on every render. Wrong shape entirely.

So ACs 3 and 8 get deferred outright, no interim. And that's cheap here in a way it wasn't for 272: AC2's inline warning already tells the shopper exactly what's wrong, right at the line item. The page-level banner is a redundant summary of it. Nothing is lost by leaving it to 404.

## Two things needing an answer

**1. Where does the max actually come from?** The ACs say "the **configured** maximum of 3." What's in the code is this, at `overrides/app/pages/product-detail/index.tsx:123`:

```ts
/** Frontend-enforced limit (SFCC-196). SFCC has no platform max-order-quantity field. */
const MAX_PURCHASE_QUANTITY = 3;
```

That comment says SFCC has no platform field for this. But **SFCC-268 "PDP – Maximum Purchase Quantity – BM Config" is marked Ready for SIT** — done, Sprint 3, Victor's. Both can't be right. Either 268 delivered a BM setting the frontend should now be reading and that constant is stale, or 268 concluded there's no field and the constant *is* the implementation despite the card's title.

Either way it needs promoting out of the PDP page — it's a page-local const today, so the cart can't reach it, and re-typing `3` in the cart breaks the no-magic-numbers rule in `conventions.md`.

**2. Does basket merge cap server-side, or do we post-process?** Merge happens on login, server-side. AC5 says the quantity is "automatically capped" — but nothing says by whom. `cart.md` §3 confirms merge happens (CFD-006) and is silent on the cap. If it's on us, the cart has to inspect the merged basket and issue corrective update calls, which is real work with real ordering concerns.

## One thing that argues for your bundle

272's guest→auth wishlist resume and 250's merge-cap **fire on the same event** — a guest authenticating from the cart. Sign in to move something to your wishlist, and the basket merges at that same moment. If that item's quantity gets capped during the merge, 272's "move all units" moves a different number than the shopper saw when they clicked.

Neither card mentions the other. Seven separate builds would each miss it; one plan across them catches it.

## Reuse already in the repo

`product-view` already implements this enforcement shape — `maxOrderQuantity?: number | null`, summed against basket line items for the variant, `null` meaning unrestricted, with tests and stories at 2, 3 and null. Portable straight to the cart item.

content.text:
**What 250 actually is:** stop a shopper putting more than 3 of the same size in their bag, and tell them why without blocking their checkout.

**What you build:** the rule. When a line item hits 3 — grey out the `+`, leave the `–` alone, show a line of text under the stepper saying the limit's reached for that size, and leave the Checkout button working. Hitting the limit isn't an error, it's just a ceiling.

**What you don't build:** the stepper (that's 271) or the warning text component (that's 795). 250 is only the logic deciding when those switch on. Nine ACs because the guest-signs-in case repeats the same three behaviours.

**Question 1 — what is "3"?**

Right now it's typed into the PDP page as `MAX_PURCHASE_QUANTITY = 3`, with a comment saying SFCC has no field for it. But SFCC-268, titled "Maximum Purchase Quantity – **BM Config**", is marked done. Both can't be true.

Guess wrong and you type `3` into the cart as well. Then the day someone changes it to 2, you have two places to find and one of them gets missed. Victor owned 268 — he can settle it in a sentence.

**Question 2 — who caps the merge?**

A guest with 2 in their bag signs into an account that already has 2. The server combines the bags. Does it stop at 3, or hand back 4?

This is the one that matters. Assume the server caps when it doesn't, and a shopper walks away with 4 in their bag and can order 4 — past a limit the business set. And it only happens on a guest-signs-in path, which is exactly the path nobody thinks to test.

Assume the *opposite* and you write correction code that fights the server. So it's not a safe thing to guess in either direction.

That one's an integration question, not a frontend one.

**Neither blocks starting.** ACs 1, 2, 4, 6, 7 and 9 don't depend on either answer. Build those, and leave the merge cap until someone confirms who owns it.

content.text:
Both answered with evidence. Neither needs a human.

## Q1 — there is no configured max. The constant *is* the implementation.

Two checks, same answer:

**SCAPI type surface** — `commerce-sdk-isomorphic`'s generated types contain `minOrderQuantity` (6 occurrences) and `stepQuantity`. **No `maxOrderQuantity` anywhere.** SFCC has no standard field for this.

**Live dev sandbox** (`ZimmermannAU`, two real products) — quantity keys returned are `inventory`, `minOrderQuantity`, `stepQuantity`. `maxOrderQuantity` absent. And the custom attributes coming through are:

`c_ap21Category` · `c_careInstructions` · `c_countryOfOrigin` · `c_environmentalNotes` · `c_fabricComposition` · `c_hsCode` · `c_isFinalSale` · `c_isNew` · `c_isSale` · `c_label` · `c_relatedMasterProductID` · `c_season` · `c_sizeFit` · `c_sizeGuide` · `c_styleId` · `c_styleNumber` · `c_stylingNotes` · `c_relatedSwatches` · `c_showEnvironmentalNote`

Nineteen of them, none quantity-related. So custom-attribute exposure is working fine — the max just isn't there.

**So:** `MAX_PURCHASE_QUANTITY = 3` in the PDP page is the real enforcement, and its comment is accurate. For 250, promote it out of `product-detail/index.tsx` into a shared constant so the cart reads the same value instead of re-typing `3`.

**Side finding worth a word with Victor:** SFCC-268 is titled "Maximum Purchase Quantity – **BM Config**" and is marked Ready for SIT, but nothing reachable from the Shopper API was configured. 250's ACs all say "the **configured** maximum of 3." Either 268's title is misleading or something was configured that the PWA can't see. Worth a comment on the card so the next person doesn't go looking for a setting that isn't there.

## Q2 — the server already prevents it. ACs 5–9 describe something that can't happen.

`mergeBasket` takes `productItemMergeMode` with four values — `higher_quantity`, `sum_quantities`, `saved_quantity`, `separate_item` — and the SDK docs state the default plainly: *"the higher of the two basket quantities is used for each product."*

All four merge call sites in the base app — `use-auth-modal`, `login`, `social-login-redirect`, `checkout/contact-info` — pass **only** `createDestinationBasket: true`. No merge mode. So the default applies everywhere.

**Guest has 2, account has 2 → merged basket has 2.** Not 4. Quantities never sum.

AC5's premise is *"the combined quantity of the same SKU exceeds the maximum"* — that's summing. It doesn't occur. The only route to a basket over 3 is one that was already over 3, which PDP enforcement blocks at add-to-cart.

**But AC5's intent is still worth building** — "it never displays a quantity exceeding the maximum" is sound. Just don't build it as merge logic. Build it as a render-time guard: if any line item exceeds max, cap and flag it, regardless of how it got there. That covers stale baskets, baskets predating enforcement, anything created through BM or order-on-behalf, and it survives someone later switching the merge mode. Broader coverage, less code, and no dependency on the login event.

## Where that leaves 250

**7 of 9 buildable now**, 2 deferred to 404 (the page-level banner), **0 unknowns**.

Two caveats, stated plainly: I probed the **dev** sandbox and two products, so a custom attribute on sit/uat isn't ruled out — though with no standard field at all, that'd be surprising. And if anyone ever passes `sum_quantities`, the merge conclusion flips and AC5 becomes real.

The probe script is in the scratchpad, not the repo — nothing added to the codebase.
