content.text:
You were right, and here's what I missed.

The merge only applies `higher_quantity` to items it considers **the same product**. The match requires *all* of these to be equal:

> shipment · productId · option values · wishlist reference · inventory list id · gift flag & message · ad-hoc price adjustments

And then: *"If any of the listed values don't match, then the item in the previous shopper's basket is copied to a **new line item** in the current shopper's basket."*

So:

- Guest basket: 2 × SKU-X
- Account basket: 2 × SKU-X, **different shipment** (or different inventory list, or one has a gift message)
- Merge → **two line items, 4 units of SKU-X in the basket**

`higher_quantity` never fired, because they weren't the same product. The cap is exceeded.

**And the codebase already assumes exactly this.** The PDP's own enforcement:

```ts
const inBag = basketProductItems
  .filter((item) => item.productId === productId)
  .reduce((sum, item) => sum + (item.quantity ?? 0), 0);
```

It sums across line items filtered by `productId`. You only write that if the same SKU can occupy more than one line. I read the existing code and still missed what it was telling me.

**AC5's wording was more precise than my reading of it.** It says the *"**combined** quantity of the same SKU exceeds the maximum"* — combined across line items. I read it as "the merge sums them," which is where I went wrong.

**And it's not theoretical for this project.** Three of those match fields are live Zimmermann scope: **shipment** (BOPIS / Collect in Boutique creates separate shipments), **inventory list id** (boutique vs warehouse stock, per CAI-022's MuleSoft routing), and **gift flag & message**. Any of those differing between the two baskets splits the line.

## Revised verdict

`higher_quantity` protects only the single-line case. **AC5 is real.** I was wrong to call ACs 5–9 unreachable.

The fix I proposed still stands and is now clearly right: a render-time guard summing per-SKU across line items, mirroring what the PDP already does. It covers the merge case and every other route to an over-max basket, without hooking the login event.

AC5 says the quantity is *"automatically capped at 3"* and *"never **displays** a quantity exceeding the maximum."*

With 4 units split as 2 + 2 across two line items, **neither line displays more than 3.** So is the basket compliant or not?

- The PDP treats the limit as **per SKU across the basket** — it sums.

If it's per-SKU, capping means reducing *something* — and the AC doesn't say which line, or whether to reduce at all versus just disable `+` and warn. And no Figma covers "you have 4 of this across two lines, the cap is 3."

Good idea. Here's the three-way.

## Behaviour by behaviour

| Behaviour | Card / ACs ask for | Server (SFCC) does | Frontend already does |
|---|---|---|---|
| A max purchase quantity exists | "the **configured** maximum of 3" | **Nothing.** No `maxOrderQuantity` field, standard or custom — verified in SCAPI types and on the live dev sandbox | `MAX_PURCHASE_QUANTITY = 3`, a hardcoded const in the PDP page |
| Block going over the limit | Disable `+` at the limit | Nothing | Hard-blocks Add to Bag and caps `QuantityPicker`'s `max` |
| How "at the limit" is measured | Quantity **equals** 3, per line item | n/a | `inBag >= max`, **summed per SKU across all line items** |
| Correct a basket already over the limit | AC5: "automatically **capped** at 3" | Nothing | **Nothing** — it prevents, it never reduces |
| Merge two baskets | AC5: combined qty > 3 gets capped | `higher_quantity` for matching items; **non-matching items become separate line items** | Nothing — no cart override exists |
| Inline warning at the line item | "Maximum purchase quantity reached for this size" + icon | n/a | Nothing in cart; 795 will provide it |
| Page-level banner | "An item in your bag has reached maximum quantity" | n/a | Nothing; 404 will provide it |
| Checkout stays enabled | ACs 4, 9 | n/a | n/a — Apple/Google Pay buttons don't exist yet (SFCC-309) |

## What that actually tells us

**The server contributes nothing to this feature.** Not a limit, not enforcement, not validation. So there's no server-versus-ACs conflict to reconcile — the only real comparison is **the ACs versus the frontend's own existing rule**, and that rule was invented on the PDP.

Which reframes 250 entirely. It isn't "wire the cart up to a configured limit." It's **"extend the frontend's self-imposed limit to a second surface, and make the two agree."**

And on two points the existing frontend is *more* correct than the ACs:

**`>=` versus `equals`.** ACs 1 and 2 say the quantity *"equals* the configured maximum of 3." The PDP uses `inBag >= max`. If a basket ever holds 4 — which the split-line merge case makes possible — then `== 3` is false, so the `+` stays live and no warning shows. The ACs are written assuming a basket can never be above max. It can.

**Per-SKU versus per-line.** The PDP sums across line items. The ACs are written per line item — "that line item," "beneath the quantity stepper." Those two disagree the moment the same SKU occupies two lines.

And on one point the ACs ask for something **neither** the server nor the frontend has ever done: AC5's *auto-cap*. The PDP prevents going over; it never reduces an existing quantity. Auto-capping means issuing a corrective basket write on render, which is new behaviour with a different risk shape — write loops, and a race with the merge that triggered it.

## So the decisions are

1. **Is the limit per line item or per SKU across the basket?** PDP says per-SKU. Cart ACs read per-line. Pick one and make both surfaces match.
2. **`>=` or `==`?** Follow the PDP and use `>=`, which means the cart handles over-max baskets the ACs don't describe.
3. **Auto-cap, or flag-only?** AC5 says cap. Nothing in the codebase reduces quantities today. Flag-and-disable is the lower-risk read of "never displays a quantity exceeding the maximum" — and with 2+2 across two lines, no line displays over 3 anyway.
4. **Promote the constant** so both surfaces read one value. That one you've already called.

1, 2 and 4 you can decide. **3 is the only one I'd put to whoever wrote the card**, because "capped" is a commercial decision about silently changing what's in someone's bag.

And `cart.md` §2 settles the per-line-vs-per-SKU question you and I were circling:

> **Max 3 units per SKU** (same size + colour) **per order**

"Per order" means per basket, not per line. So summing across line items is right, the PDP is already correct, and the ACs' per-line framing is the loose one.

Three things follow from "reduce to 3" that the AC doesn't answer.

**Which line loses the units?** Guest had 2, account had 2, different shipments → 4 total, shed 1. From which line? Those lines differ precisely *because* something about fulfilment differs — shipment, or inventory list. So reducing the guest's line versus the account's line can change whether the shopper gets that unit by delivery or by boutique pickup. That's a commercial call, not a technical one.

**What if reducing hits zero?** Guest had 1, account had 3 → 4 total, shed 1, and the guest's line goes to 0. Do you delete the line? AC5 says "capped at 3" — it doesn't say "line removed." Deleting a line the shopper added is more aggressive than trimming a quantity, and it's a different mutation.

**Does the shopper get told?** This is the one I'd push on. Neither AC's copy discloses a change. The inline warning says "Maximum purchase quantity reached for this size." The banner says "An item in your bag has reached maximum quantity." Both describe a *state*. Neither says **"we removed one from your bag."**

So as specified, you'd silently reduce what someone put in their bag and tell them only that they're at a limit. That's the kind of thing that generates a complaint, and it also means my earlier call — "defer the banner to 404, nothing is lost" — was too relaxed. If a silent mutation is happening, the disclosure matters more, and right now no AC provides one.

**One implementation point while we're here.** Do the capping at cart render, not by hooking the merge.

`mergeBasket` is called from four base files — `use-auth-modal`, `login`, `social-login-redirect`, `checkout/contact-info`. Hooking the merge means overriding all four to catch every path. A guard in the cart that acts whenever it sees an over-max SKU covers all four merge routes plus any other way a basket gets over the limit, and touches no base files.

**What goes wrong.** A guest with 2 of a dress in their bag signs in. Their account already has 2 of the same dress. Normally the two bags combine and the server keeps the bigger number, 2 — it never adds them. But if the two are in the bag *differently* — one set for delivery, one for boutique pickup — the server sees them as two different things and keeps both rows. The shopper now has 4 of that dress. Over the limit.

**What you want:** spot that the total is 4 and bring it down to 3.

Three things nobody has decided.

**Which row loses one?** The rows exist *because* they're fulfilled differently. Take one off the pickup row and the shopper loses a boutique collection. Take it off the delivery row and they lose a delivery. That's a business call — not something to decide in code.

**What if a row empties?** Guest had 1, account had 3. Getting to 3 means taking the guest's single unit away, and now that row has nothing in it. Do you delete the row? The card says "capped," not "removed." Deleting a row the shopper added is a bigger move than trimming a number, and it's a different operation.

**Does the shopper find out?** This is the one that worries me most. Both messages the card asks for say a version of *"you've reached the limit."* Neither says *"we took one out of your bag."*

So as written: someone puts 4 in their bag, signs in, and quietly ends up with 3 — told only that they're at a limit, never that anything changed. That's a complaint waiting to happen.

It also means what I said earlier was too casual. I said skipping the page-level banner costs nothing because the line-level warning covers it. If we're silently changing what's in someone's bag, how we tell them matters *more*, not less — and right now neither message does that job.

**Where the code goes.** The bag-combining happens in four different places in the base template — the sign-in popup, the login page, the return from social sign-in, and checkout. Catch it at the combine and you'd have to override all four.

Instead, have the cart check itself every time it draws: *does any item total more than 3? then fix it.* One place, covers all four routes, and covers anything else that ever leaves a bag over the limit.

content.text:
Two corrections first — one of them changes what you're building.

## Where delivery-vs-boutique came from: I was wrong for plain cart

You're right to challenge it. Every basket has a shipment, but at plain cart stage — no delivery method chosen, no Collect in Boutique selected — both baskets' items sit in the same default shipment and the same default inventory list. They **match**. So my 4-unit example doesn't happen at plain cart.

It needs something to have already differentiated the two baskets. The realistic one for this project is Collect in Boutique, which assigns a different shipment and boutique inventory list — but that's a fulfilment choice the shopper has to have made. Not the default case.

## The bigger one: 2 + 2 is 2, not 4

You said "guest with 2 and signed-in with 2 is 4 and will be reduced to 3." **The server doesn't add them.** Default mode is `higher_quantity` — it takes the larger of the two numbers. Guest 2, account 2 → the merged bag holds **2**.

So there's nothing to reduce. The cap logic would never fire in the case you just described.

And your other example is already correct without any code: guest 1, account 3 → the server keeps 3, one row, guest's row gone. That's exactly what you described as wanting, and it's what happens today.

**So the real question isn't "how do we cap the merge." It's "should the merge add at all?"**

- `higher_quantity` (today's default) — bigger of the two wins. 2+2 → 2.
- `sum_quantities` — adds them. 2+2 → 4. **This is what AC5 is written for.**
- `saved_quantity` — the logged-in bag always wins. Closest to your "logged-in preferred."

AC5's wording — "the **combined** quantity ... exceeds the maximum" — only makes sense under `sum_quantities`. Whoever wrote it assumed adding. Commercially that's arguably right: someone who put 2 in as a guest and had 2 saved probably wants 4, capped to 3 — not silently dropped to 2.

But nobody has passed that parameter. So either the AC assumes a mode we don't use, or the mode needs changing. **That's the decision under this whole thread**, and it's a product one.

Disclosure — noted, out of scope, dropping it.

## Your question: override the four, or have the cart check itself?

**Overriding the four is worse, for three reasons.**

*You'd be adopting four Salesforce files as your own, permanently.* Copy-first means each one gets copied into `overrides/`, converted, verified, then changed. From then on, every upstream version bump means re-reconciling Salesforce's changes to four files by hand. One of them, `use-auth-modal`, is already a Tier 2 shared hook with five-plus consumers — changing it is a both-squads coordination, not a cart task.

*Two of the four aren't yours.* The login page and checkout's contact-info belong to other parts of the app. A cart story reaching into checkout to change how sign-in behaves is scope sprawl of exactly the kind the rules exist to stop.

*And you can still miss one.* Patch four paths and a fifth appears — added by an upstream bump, or by a flow nobody's built yet — and your fix quietly doesn't cover it. You'd never get a signal.

**The cart checking itself is better because it fixes a state, not an event.**

You don't have to catch every door the shopper came through. The cart looks at what's actually in the bag and asks one question: does any item total more than three? If yes, fix it. That's true no matter which of the four merge paths ran, and it's equally true for a bag that went over the limit some way nobody has thought of yet — a stale session, a CS agent placing an order on someone's behalf.

One file, inside your own story's boundary, nothing borrowed from Salesforce, nothing to re-reconcile later.

**Two honest costs.** It corrects on render, so a shopper could see 4 for a moment before it settles — and you need a guard so it doesn't re-fire in a loop.

**And one real gap you should know about:** checkout's contact-info also triggers a merge. If someone signs in *during checkout* and never opens the cart, a cart-only check never runs and checkout sees 4.

So build it as a small shared utility the cart calls — not logic buried inside the cart component. Then when checkout gets built, it calls the same one. Same answer, one implementation, and you're not back overriding four base files to get there.

content.text:
## First, a finding that changes Q1 and Q3

**No Zimmermann code merges baskets at all**, and the SDK doesn't do it for you — `mergeBasket` appears in `commerce-sdk-react` only as a mutation definition, never in its `auth/` code. It has to be called explicitly, and only the four base files call it.

Which means the cart's own sign-in path doesn't merge. `useWishlistAuthDrawer` logs in via `LoginPasswordlessUser` and `AuthorizeIDP` and never calls merge. The social route survives by accident — it redirects through the base `social-login-redirect` page, which does merge. **The email-code route doesn't.** So a guest with items who signs in from the cart with an email code has their guest bag orphaned, not merged.

That's a defect in what's already shipped, and it sits directly under both 272 and 250.

## Q1 — yes, `sum_quantities` is what AC5 is written for

"Combined quantity ... exceeds the maximum" only works if quantities add. Confirmed.

But the mode is a **request parameter**, so it can only be passed where `mergeBasket` is called — and there's no Zimmermann call site to put it in. Two ways out:

**Add a Zimmermann-owned merge call in the cart's sign-in flow.** You arguably need one anyway, given the finding above. That call is your code, so it passes `sum_quantities` and caps immediately after. No base files touched.

**Or override the base four** to make every entry point consistent.

The tension: take the first and merge behaviour differs by where you signed in — summed from the cart, higher-of-two from the login page or checkout. Same shopper, different bag depending on the door they came through. That inconsistency is arguably worse than either mode on its own.

So AC5 isn't buildable until someone decides **who owns the merge call and whether the mode changes everywhere or just in the cart.** That's the real dependency under this whole thread — not the capping logic.

## Q2 — the flash, and what the guard is for

**Preventing the flash.** Two options:

*Block until settled* — treat an over-max basket as "reconciling" and show the cart's loading state until the correction lands. The shopper never sees a number that isn't real. Costs a brief spinner, and this only happens when a guest with items signs in and the sum exceeds three, so it's rare.

*Derive the display* — show `min(actual, 3)` and correct the server in the background. No spinner. But the UI then says 3 while the server holds 4, and if that write fails you're showing a number that isn't true — and checkout would charge for 4.

I'd block. It never displays a false quantity, and it matches the project's standing rule to surface a problem rather than paper over it.

**What the guard is for — two different failures.**

*Concurrent writes.* A render sees 4 and fires the correction. Before it resolves, another render still sees 4 and fires a second one. Two writes hit the same line item, last one wins, and the final quantity can land wrong.

*Runaway retries.* The correction completes, the cart re-renders, checks again — and it's *still* over max, because the server rejected the update or there were three lines and one pass wasn't enough. Unguarded, that loops forever, and every lap is a network write. You'd hammer the API and possibly get the shopper rate-limited.

So the guard is: one correction in flight at a time, one attempt per basket version, and if it's still over after that, stop and show an error instead of spinning.

## Q3 — no, the shared utility doesn't prevent that gap

Being straight with you: it prevents **divergence**, not the gap. The utility only runs where something calls it. If checkout never calls it, checkout still sees 4.

What it buys you is one implementation instead of two that drift apart.

Closing the gap needs the check to actually run on the checkout path, and that's checkout's story to build, not 250's. What 250 can do is ship the utility, call it from the cart, and write the requirement into the checkout story so it gets picked up rather than rediscovered later.

**Though if the merge call does end up Zimmermann-owned** — per Q1 — then cap right after the merge inside that call. It's covered wherever that call runs, whichever surface rendered, and the checkout gap closes as a side effect rather than needing its own fix.

content.text:
## The shipped defect — what to do

**Prove it first.** I inferred it from reading code. Verify live: guest adds an item, opens the cart, signs in with the email code, check whether the item survives. Your own standing rule — a finding isn't real until you've made it fail on purpose.

**Then file it** against the wishlist auth drawer lineage (SFCC-742/926), not against 250 or 272. It's pre-existing, it's not theirs.

**But build the merge call inside this build anyway**, because both cards need it:

- 272's AC8 says the guest authenticates and *then the item moves from the cart to the wishlist*. If the guest's cart was orphaned at sign-in, there's no item left to move. The defect breaks AC8 outright.
- 250's AC5 needs a merge to exist at all.

So it isn't an adjacent bug to note and walk past. It's load-bearing for two of your seven.

## Q1 — the call

Checked: there's **no login page override**, and the checkout override is only `partials/payment.tsx`. So all four merge call sites are still base, and Zimmermann owns none of them.

**Recommendation: add a Zimmermann-owned merge call in the cart's sign-in flow, pass `sum_quantities`, cap immediately after.**

You're writing that call regardless — the defect means the cart's email-code sign-in doesn't merge at all today. The mode and the cap ride along for free.

The alternative means adopting four Salesforce files from a cart story: `use-auth-modal` (a Tier 2 shared hook with five-plus consumers, so both-squads coordination), the base login page, the social redirect page, and checkout's contact-info. You'd own all four permanently and re-reconcile them on every upstream bump.

And the inconsistency fails in the safe direction — cart sign-in sums, the other doors take higher-of-two. A shopper signing in elsewhere gets *fewer* items, not corrupted ones.

**The honest counter:** login and checkout are the busier doors, so the correct behaviour would sit on the quieter one. That's a real argument — but it's an argument for a follow-up story that routes every sign-in surface through one Zimmermann merge call, not for four overrides inside a cart ticket.

## Q2 — no action on the flash, but the guard is a different thing

Flash: agreed, leave it and observe. It's cosmetic, rare, and costs nothing to skip.

But the loop guard wasn't in what you quoted, and it isn't the same risk. The flash means a shopper sees a wrong number for a moment. The loop means the cart writes to the server, re-renders, sees the same problem, writes again — indefinitely. Every lap is a network call. That can rate-limit a shopper out of their own basket.

I'd keep the guard even with no flash handling. Your call, but worth deciding separately rather than as part of "no action."

## Q3 — explained plainly

**A shared utility is a tool, not a tripwire.** Putting the rule in a shared function means the cart and checkout *can* apply the identical rule. It doesn't mean either of them *will*. Someone has to pick it up and call it. Miss that, and that surface has no check — the function sitting there unused changes nothing.

So a shared utility solves a different problem than the one you're worried about. It stops the cart and checkout drifting into two slightly different versions of the rule. It does not make checkout safe.

**Fixing at the merge is different in kind.** The merge is the one moment an over-sized bag gets created. Nothing reaches the cart or checkout without passing through it. Fix it there and every surface downstream inherits the fix, whether or not anyone remembered to add a check.

Checking in the cart is like reading the label on every shelf in the shop. Fixing at the merge is weighing the trolley once, at the door.

**And the catch: you can only fix the door if you own it.** Today Salesforce owns all four. That's why the defect matters beyond itself — the cart's sign-in needs its own merge call built regardless, and once that exists, it's *your* door. The fix goes inside it, and checkout stops being a gap you have to remember about.

content.text:
Eight ACs. Reuse is strong, but two of them have nowhere to route to.

## The 8

| # | AC | Status |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Domestic: Checkout CTA (primary, full-width black) → Apple Pay (outlined) → Google Pay (outlined) | ✅ — but overlaps SFCC-309 |
| 2 | International: Apple/Google Pay hidden, content shifts up, no white gap | ✅ |
| 3 | Error in cart → buttons stay **visually enabled**, "blocked at backend level" | ⚠️ not a frontend deliverable |
| 4 | Errors resolved → block removed, buttons process | ⚠️ same |
| 5 | Domestic, any auth status → straight to checkout | ✅ |
| 6 | International **guest** → intermediate login page (SFCC-880) | ❌ no destination |
| 7 | International **authenticated** → straight to Global-e (SFCC-63) | ❌ no destination |
| 8 | Responsive across desktop/tablet/mobile per Figma | ✅ |

## Reuse is unusually good here

**ZimmButton already has both variants AC1 needs** — `primary` and `secondary` (the outlined one), alongside `primaryInverse`, `secondaryInverse`, `social`, `icon`, `iconInverse`. No atom gap, which is a change from SFCC-588/590/347.

**The domestic/international branch is already built and documented for this exact use.** `useCountryConfig` returns a `CountryConfig` with `checkoutOwner`, and its own doc comment says:

> Checkout owner for this site's domestic path. Branch checkout AND pricing logic from this field at **PDP/cart level** — not only at the checkout page.

That's written for 275. ACs 2, 5, 6 and 7's branch is a config read, not new logic.

## Three real problems

**AC3/AC4 assert backend behaviour in a UI story, and specify no feedback.** The card calls itself "a PWA Kit UI component story." Backend blocking isn't in that. Worse — the AC never says what the shopper *sees* when they click an enabled button that doesn't work. As written: click, nothing happens. That's worse than a disabled button, and it cuts against the project's rule to surface an explicit error rather than silently doing nothing.

275 can deliver the half it owns: buttons render enabled during error states. The blocking belongs elsewhere, and the feedback isn't specified anywhere at all.

**ACs 6 and 7 have no destination.** SFCC-880, the intermediate login page, is **To Do, unassigned, no sprint** — worse placed than 404, which at least has you and a sprint. And Global-e is "Not started" in `projectState.md`, with PRC-43 and PRC-46 still open. So the international routing half of this card cannot complete.

**Scope overlap with SFCC-309.** 275 says it covers three buttons including Apple and Google Pay. SFCC-309 is titled "Cart Page – Google Pay Express and Apple Pay Express Buttons" — To Do, unassigned, no sprint, and carrying **the same `CAI-010` label as 275**. Two cards, same requirement ID, overlapping subject. Does 275 render those two buttons, or only the Checkout CTA plus slots for 309 to fill? Unsettled, and it produces either duplicate work or a hole.

## One cross-card thing

275's AC3 lists "quantity error requiring customer action" as a blocking condition. 250's ACs 4 and 9 say max-quantity explicitly does **not** block checkout. Those only reconcile if max-qty isn't a "quantity error requiring customer action" — which is what 250 asserts. Worth confirming, since both cards are specifying the same button's state.

## Tally

**4 of 8 buildable now** (1, 2, 5, 8) · 2 not frontend-deliverable as written (3, 4) · 2 blocked on unowned work (6, 7).

What I'd build: the button group, domestic routing, and the `checkoutOwner` branch — with international routed to an explicit placeholder behind that branch rather than pretending. The branch is the durable part; the destination drops in when 880 and Global-e exist.

Two things to raise before building: the 309 overlap, and what the shopper actually sees in AC3.

content.text:
Noted on both — deliver 275's half of 3/4, and stop at the blocked edge on 6/7.

On 309, let me check rather than guess.

Half right. 309 is *mostly* behaviour — but it also explicitly claims rendering.

Its description:

> This story covers the Google Pay Express and Apple Pay Express **button rendering, display logic**, browser/device detection, payment flows, tokenisation, and order placement... **The Checkout CTA layout on the cart page is covered by SFCC-275.**

So 309 claims the express buttons' rendering *and* scopes 275 down to the Checkout CTA alone. 275 says the opposite — "the button group consists of three buttons," and AC1 asserts all three render in order with the outlined styling.

**But 309 settles it by being unspecified.** It says of itself: *"This is a placeholder story — full requirements, ACs, and dependencies to be defined when the Payments epic is groomed."* No ACs at all, no sprint, unassigned. 275 has eight ACs and is Ready for Development. Specified beats placeholder.

**And there's a clean seam all three cards agree on, once you spot it — there are two different hides.**

275's AC2 hides the express buttons on **international storefronts**. That's region-based, and it comes straight from `checkoutOwner` in config.

The hide that 275 disclaims — *"show/hide logic based on device/browser eligibility"* → SFCC-383/384 — is **device-based**. Different input, different card.

So the split that holds:

- **275** — the three buttons, fixed order, `primary` and `secondary` variants, responsive, and the region-based hide. Presentation.
- **309 / 383 / 384** — device and browser eligibility, payment flow, tokenisation, order placement. Behaviour.

Which is your hypothesis, just with the line drawn at region-vs-device rather than render-vs-behaviour.

**Action:** build 275 as written, and put a comment on 309 recording that 275 delivers the button presentation and the region hide — so when the Payments epic gets groomed, 309 starts from behaviour only instead of re-specifying buttons that already exist.

One thing to carry forward: 309 also flags an unanswered question — *"confirm which storefronts support G Pay and Apple Pay."* Doesn't block 275, since AC2's rule is simply "not on international," but it'll matter to whoever grooms 309.

content.text:
Group A. Three decisions in it, and everything else is already answered.

## Decision 1 — `equals 3` or `3 or more`?

ACs 1 and 2 both say the quantity *"**equals** the configured maximum of 3."* The PDP uses `inBag >= max`.

The difference matters because a basket *can* end up holding 4. With `== 3`, four units means the condition is false — so the `+` stays live and no warning shows, exactly when it's needed most.

**Recommendation: `>=`.** Matches the PDP, and fails safe.

## Decision 2 — per line item, or per SKU across the bag?

AC1 says disable the `+` on *"that line item."* But `cart.md` says max 3 **per order**, and the PDP sums across line items.

If the same SKU sits in two lines as 2 + 1, the SKU total is 3. Per-line, neither line has hit 3, so neither `+` is disabled — and the shopper can push it to 4. Per-SKU, both lines' `+` go disabled, because adding to either would breach the limit.

**Recommendation: per SKU.** Sum across lines, and disable `+` on every line holding that SKU once the total hits the max. The inline warning shows on each capped line, so the shopper knows why that particular `+` won't move.

## Decision 3 — AC3's banner: build or defer to 404?

**Recommendation: defer.** Nothing is being silently changed in Group A — the shopper simply can't add more, and AC2's inline warning says why, right at the line item. The page-level banner is a summary of that. Nothing is lost by leaving it to 404.

(That's different from Group B, where something *does* get silently changed. We'll come back to it there.)

## AC4 — nothing to build

It's a negative assertion: don't block checkout. So just don't add a block. It needs a Checkout CTA to assert against, which 275 provides.

## What Group A depends on

| AC | Needs | In the bundle? |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | the stepper — 271 | ✅ |
| 2 | the inline warning — 795 | ✅ |
| 3 | the banner — 404 | ❌ → defer |
| 4 | the Checkout CTA — 275 | ✅ |

So Group A is fully satisfiable from cards already in your bundle, except AC3.

Three calls to make: `>=`, per-SKU, and defer the banner.

Group A settled:

- **Per line item** — one line, one SKU, one limit
- **AC3's banner → 404**

Your reasoning on per-line holds: the SKU is already size *and* colour, so in normal shopping one line **is** one SKU, and the two readings collapse into the same thing.

**One consequence to record as deliberate, not missed.** The two readings only diverge when the same SKU occupies two lines — and the only thing that creates that is the merge splitting a line. In that case, per-line lets the SKU total pass 3: two lines at 2 each, neither at max, both `+` still live.

Which is fine, because that's exactly what AC5 in Group B exists to catch. Group A deliberately doesn't cover it.

content.text:
Group B. Banking what's already settled so we don't redo it:

- **Merge mode: `sum_quantities`** — your call, so AC5's scenario is real
- **ACs 6–9 inherit Group A's mechanics** — same `>=`, same per-line, same banner deferral, same no-block

That leaves AC5 as the only new behaviour, and one question that comes before all the others.

## What does "capped at 3" actually produce?

AC5 says the quantity is *"automatically capped at 3."* With `sum_quantities`, a guest with 2 merging into an account with 2 gives 4. Bringing that to 3 can land two ways:

**One line at 3** — the two lines consolidate, one line item, quantity 3.

**Two lines totalling 3** — e.g. 2 + 1, both lines kept.

**This matters because of the per-line decision you just made.** ACs 6 and 7 say that after capping, the `+` is disabled and the inline warning shows. Under per-line enforcement:

- One line at 3 → the line is at max → `+` disabled, warning shows. **ACs 6 and 7 pass.**
- Two lines at 2 + 1 → neither line is at max → nothing disabled, no warning. **ACs 6 and 7 silently fail**, and the shopper can push the total back to 4.

So the capping shape and Group A's per-line rule have to agree, or half of Group B doesn't work.

**Recommendation: consolidate to one line at 3.** It's what "the quantity is capped at 3" reads as, it makes 6 and 7 work without special-casing, and it matches how the merge behaves in the normal case anyway — same SKU, same shipment, one line.

That one first?

content.text:
Good news on that — the server already does it for you.

`sum_quantities` applies to items the merge treats as the same product, and the docs call the result *"the merged line item"* — singular. Guest 2 + account 2 of a matching SKU becomes **one line at 4**, not two lines. So consolidation is free; the only work is bringing that single line from 4 down to 3.

And the two-line case needs no consolidation at all: lines only stay separate when something *doesn't* match — different shipment, inventory list, gift flag — and in that case nothing summed, so each line keeps its own quantity and per-line enforcement handles it.

So your decision costs nothing to implement. It's what the platform produces anyway.

## Next thing: where does the reduction happen?

One line holding 4 needs to become 3. Two places that can happen:

**Right after the merge** — whoever calls `mergeBasket` reduces the line immediately. Covers every surface, because it's at the source. But no Zimmermann code calls `mergeBasket` today, so this means either owning a merge call or overriding base ones.

**At cart render** — the cart notices a line over max and reduces it. No base files touched, and it catches over-max baskets from any cause, not just merge. But it only runs where the cart renders.

That's the fork. Everything else in Group B — the defect, the loop guard, the checkout gap — hangs off which of these you pick, so I'd settle this one before touching any of them.

Want my recommendation, or do you want to weigh it yourself first?

**Recommendation: own a merge call in the cart — not in the shared hook, and not by overriding the base four.**

Here's the thing that decides it. You chose `sum_quantities`, and that's a **request parameter** — it only exists where `mergeBasket` is called. So a cart-render guard can't deliver it. Without a call site, the merge still runs at the default, 2 + 2 stays 2, and the guard has nothing to reduce. Option B doesn't sidestep the call-site problem; it just fails to solve it.

So a call site is required either way. The question is only whose.

**Where it goes:** the cart's own `onAuthSuccess`, passed into `useWishlistAuthDrawer`. Not inside the hook itself — that hook has three other consumers, and adding a merge there would change sign-in behaviour for the header, the PDP and the drawer menu all at once. Keep it in the cart's callback and the change stays inside 250's boundary.

That callback then does three things in order:

1. **Merge** with `sum_quantities`
2. **Reduce** any line now over max
3. **Resume** 272's pending wishlist move

The order matters — the wishlist move operates on a line item that the merge may have just consolidated and the cap may have just reduced. Do it the other way round and 272 moves a quantity the shopper never saw.

**Why not the base four:** you'd adopt `use-auth-modal` (Tier 2 shared hook, five-plus consumers, both-squads coordination), the base login page, the social redirect page, and checkout's contact-info. Four Salesforce files owned permanently and re-reconciled on every upstream bump — from a cart ticket. Two of them aren't cart territory at all.

**Add the cart-render guard as well, but as the secondary.** It's small, and it catches an over-max basket that arrived some other way — a stale session, a CS agent ordering on someone's behalf, a future path nobody's built. Primary mechanism is the merge call; the guard is the net under it.

**Two things to accept explicitly:**

The other sign-in doors keep `higher_quantity`, so merge behaviour differs by where you signed in. It fails safe — those doors give *fewer* items, not corrupted ones — and the fix is a follow-up story that routes every sign-in surface through the one Zimmermann merge call. Worth filing, not worth doing inside 250.

And this only works if the cart's sign-in actually merges, which today it doesn't. So the defect I flagged earlier stops being a separate concern and becomes step 1 of this work — you're adding the missing merge, not patching around it.

content.text:
**What happens if you don't do this.** You decided the two bags should add up — 2 and 2 makes 4, then trimmed to 3. If nobody owns the moment the bags get combined, that never happens. The bags combine the old way, the shopper ends up with 2, and the trimming code you wrote never runs because there's nothing over the limit. AC5 would look built and do nothing.

**Why it has to be at that moment.** "Add the two bags together" isn't a setting you switch on somewhere. It's an instruction you give to whoever is doing the combining, while they're doing it — like telling someone how to stack two boxes. You can't leave a note on the shelf afterwards.

Right now Salesforce's code does the combining, in four different places, and none of them says "add them." They all say "take the bigger of the two."

**And here's what makes the fix cheap.** The cart's own sign-in doesn't combine the bags *at all* today. That's the defect I found earlier. So you're not adding a second combining step — you're filling a hole that's already there.

**The fix.** When someone signs in from the cart, your code does three things in order:

1. Combine the two bags, adding the quantities
2. Trim anything now over three
3. Finish the wishlist move they were signing in for

The order isn't decoration. Step 3 acts on a line that steps 1 and 2 just changed. Do it first and you'd move a quantity the shopper never saw.

**Why not fix Salesforce's four places instead.** You'd be taking ownership of four of their files permanently — including one shared piece that five other things depend on, plus the login page and a checkout file that aren't yours. Every time Salesforce ships an update you'd hand-merge all four. That's a lot to take on from a cart ticket.

**One extra, small.** Have the cart also check itself when it draws: any line over three, trim it. That's the backstop for a bag that got too big some other way — an old session, a service agent placing an order for someone. The sign-in fix is the main thing; this is the net underneath it.

**Two knock-ons to accept out loud.** Signing in from the login page or checkout still takes the bigger of the two rather than adding — so behaviour differs by which door you came through. It errs toward *fewer* items, not wrong ones, and the tidy-up is a separate story that points every sign-in door at your one combining step.

Five, ranked. The first two are the ones I'd actually change the plan for.

## 1. The cart isn't the only door — and the other three lose the bag entirely

I've been saying "the cart's sign-in." But `useWishlistAuthDrawer` has **four** consumers: the cart (new), the header account link, the drawer menu, and the PDP. None of them merges. And no merge means the guest's basket is orphaned when the session switches — **the items are gone, not mis-counted.**

So the defect isn't "the cart doesn't merge." It's "none of the Zimmermann sign-in surfaces merge." My recommendation fixes one of four and leaves cart loss in place on the other three.

That inverts the reasoning I gave you. I argued against putting the merge inside the shared hook because three other consumers would be affected — but those three consumers have the identical gap, so the hook is arguably the *right* place, not the risky one.

And losing someone's bag is a worse bug than capping a quantity wrong. It probably outranks 250 on priority.

## 2. `sum_quantities` changes every merge, not just the over-max ones

This is the one nobody has signed off. Switching the mode doesn't only affect baskets that breach the limit — it affects **every** merge.

Guest adds one dress. Comes back a week later, signs in, and their account already had that dress. Today they get one. With `sum_quantities` they get two.

Did they mean two dresses? Almost certainly not. `higher_quantity` gets that case right and `sum_quantities` gets it wrong — and it's a far more common case than 2 + 2 breaching a cap.

So AC5's wording quietly forces a product decision with much wider reach than AC5 itself. That's worth putting to whoever wrote the card before you change the mode.

## 3. The two mechanisms I recommended fight each other

I told you to do both: trim right after the merge, *and* trim at cart render. They overlap on exactly the same event. The merge sets the line to 4, the callback starts trimming, the cart re-renders, sees 4, and starts trimming too. Two writes on the same line item, and the losing one can leave the quantity wrong.

If you keep both, the render guard has to stand down while a merge is in flight. That's my recommendation creating the very race I warned you about two messages ago.

## 4. It welds 250 and 272 together

One callback doing merge → cap → resume the wishlist move means 250's code and 272's code live in the same function. They can't be built, reviewed, or reverted separately.

That cuts directly against the staged-PR shape I proposed at the start — where each story keeps its own PR and its own Jira key. Worth knowing before you plan the branches.

## 5. You can't fully prove it this sprint

The over-max merge needs a guest basket and an account basket with overlapping SKUs on a real sandbox — doable. But the social route can't be tested at all while Apple and Google merchant accounts are unprovisioned, and the email-code route depends on OTP working on that sandbox. So partial verification, with the gap on the path most likely to behave differently.

Yes — and the code refines it in a way that shrinks my constraint #1 considerably.

Base's own comment on the merge:

> we only want to merge basket when the user is logged in as a **recurring user** — only recurring users trigger the login mutation, new user triggers register mutation

So the invariant isn't "merge at every auth entry point." It's **"merge on login of a recurring user, deliberately not on register."** The reason holds up: a brand-new customer has no prior basket, so their guest basket simply becomes theirs — nothing to merge.

Apply that to the drawer's three routes:

| Route | Merges? | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| Social IDP | Yes — redirects through base `social-login-redirect`, which merges | ✅ fine |
| Create account | No — opens base's register view, which deliberately skips it | ✅ correct by design |
| **Passwordless OTP** | **No** | ❌ **the gap** |

**So I overstated it.** It isn't four surfaces losing the bag. It's **one route** — and it's the one route that is a recurring-user login, which is exactly the case the invariant exists for.

And the diagnosis is sharper than "a missing call." Base `use-auth-modal` has its *own* passwordless login flow, and it pairs that flow with the merge. `useWishlistAuthDrawer` reimplemented passwordless login for the drawer and didn't carry the merge across. That's the defect: a reimplementation that dropped one half of a paired behaviour.

**Which makes the fix small and well-placed.** It goes right where `loginPasswordless.mutateAsync` succeeds, inside `useWishlistAuthDrawer` — the same position base puts it relative to its own passwordless flow. One addition, matching an established pattern, and all four consumers are covered at once.

So the "don't touch the shared hook" worry I raised dissolves. You're not changing behaviour for three unrelated consumers; you're completing a behaviour that was half-implemented for all of them.

content.text:
All four done. Three are clean; 795 is the problem.

## SFCC-315 — Drawer (Cart Variation) · 9 ACs · all clean

Header text ("BAG • [count]" / "YOUR BAG IS EMPTY"), dynamic count, slide-in from the right with overlay, full-screen on mobile, close via X / outside-click / Escape with focus return, no loss of page state or scroll position, responsive.

**Reuse is strong.** `ZimmDrawer` already has `finalFocusRef` (AC7's focus return), the overlay, right placement, size variants, the mobile full-height fix and concurrent-instance scroll-lock coordination — all from SFCC-831 and 926. The dynamic count in AC3 comes free from basket cache invalidation, same mechanism as everything else.

**One clean split worth noting:** AC2 gives 315 the empty *header* text. The empty *body* — render order and logic — is 277's. So your "build it simply now" decision applies to the body only; the header line is specified here and buildable.

## SFCC-270 — Cart Item UI Part 1 · 9 ACs · all clean

Pure presentation: image, name right of image, price, colour, size, quantity with `+`/`–` either side, all items individually identifiable, Remove and Wishlist as underlined text links below the stepper, nothing truncated on mobile.

**One architectural decision though.** Base `product-item` is imported by `pages/cart`, `pages/account/wishlist`, and `product-item-list`. So it's a genuine shared SFCC internal — and `protectedFiles.md` puts it at Tier 2, **Squad B-owned**.

Overriding it means keeping the default export API-compatible for those three consumers and putting Zimmermann styling behind a named export, per the bridge pattern in `overrideStyling.md`. Building a new `ZimmCartItem` organism instead keeps it in Squad A's territory with no compatibility constraint — and it's coherent with 315 being a new organism rather than an override of base `pages/cart`.

The cost of the second route: the account wishlist page keeps base styling, so cart line items and wishlist line items would look different until someone does that page.

## SFCC-271 — Quantity Stepper · 4 ACs · all clean

Increment, decrement, `–` disabled at quantity 1, and the drawer count plus order summary updating without a page load. Confirms the correction from earlier — no SFCC-274 dependency; the summary updates through basket invalidation.

## SFCC-795 — Cart Item UI Part 2 · the problem card

Seven groups: default state, stepper states, error states, promotional price, warning state, responsive, and **eleven accessibility ACs**. Four findings.

**1. It restates three other cards.** Its "Default State" AC is 270's entire scope. Its stepper-state ACs duplicate 271's AC3 (`–` disabled at 1) and 250's AC1 (`+` disabled at max). So building 270, 271, 250 and 795 means implementing the same rules from three directions. Good for a bundle — one implementation satisfies all — but the ACs can't be signed off independently, and Zephyr would count the same coverage three times.

**2. The error states belong to cards you don't have.** Out of Stock, Partially OOS and Unavailable have their copy and rendering specified here, but the triggering logic is SFCC-282 and SFCC-796 — both Sprint 6, Tech design, Hazel's. Same shape as 250 and 404: presentation here, logic elsewhere. Buildable as states with stories; not provable end to end.

**3. The promotional state needs data that doesn't exist yet.** "Was $X / Now $Y" plus a discount label like "20% off applied" needs real promotion data on basket line items. `projectState.md` has the promotions engine and FX pricebooks still pending.

**4. A concrete conflict, and this one's checkable.** The accessibility AC requires **44×44px** touch targets on mobile for the stepper controls and both links. `ZimmButton`'s `icon` size is `minW`/`minH: var(--zimm-scale-xl)`, and `spacing.ts` resolves `xl` to `1.5rem` — **24px**.

The atom fails that AC by 20px. And 24×24 isn't an accident: it's exactly WCAG 2.2 AA's minimum target size, so the atom was built to the project standard.

Meanwhile 795 cites **WCAG 2.1 AA** as its bar — but 44×44 is 2.1 **AAA**, not AA. And `AGENTS.md` targets 2.2 AA. So the card asks for a AAA-level size while labelling it AA, against a project standard of 2.2 AA.

Either the AC relaxes to 24px, or `ZimmButton`'s icon size grows — and that's a shared atom change hitting every icon button in the app, not a cart change.

---

## Tally across the four

**315, 270, 271 — 22 ACs, all buildable.** 795 is buildable as presentation, with error states unprovable until 282/796, the promotional state unprovable until promotions exist, and one accessibility AC in direct conflict with a shared atom.

Two things to raise: the 44px-vs-24px target size, and whether 795's overlap with 270/271/250 is intentional layering or duplication that should be trimmed.

## 3. Was/Now — you're right, it exists

Base `display-price` takes `priceData` with `listPrice`, `currentPrice` and `isOnSale`, renders a `ListPrice` sub-component for the struck-through value, and already multiplies by quantity (`price={listPrice * quantity}`) — so it's line-item aware out of the box. And `cart.md` CAI-013 confirms sale was/now is in scope and price-book sourced, so the data's there too.

**So the discount label is the only new thing, and yes — purely presentational.** Prop-driven, covered by stories, wired to real data when promotions land. Nothing blocked.

One note: `display-price` has no override yet and it's a shared SFCC internal (base cart, wishlist page, product-item-list all reach it). If the cart needs Zimmermann was/now styling, that's the bridge pattern — faithful default export, styling in a recipe, no named-export split needed for token theming.

## 4. Found the precedent

`zimmButton.css.ts` has it in two places, and it's more specific than I'd assumed.

The 24px isn't a default anyone fell into — the comment reads *"WCAG 2.2 AA SC 2.5.8 — 24px minimum target size. SFCC-55's accessibility note names this control specifically."* So it was chosen deliberately, against a named criterion, with the story that asked for it recorded next to it. There's also a long note explaining why it's `minW`/`minH` rather than padding (Chakra's `IconButton` hard-sets `padding: 0` as a style prop, so any padding declared there is silently dropped — a previous `p: 'xs'` rendered 16×16).

And the focus-ring annotation shows the same shape: cite the criterion (2.4.7), say what the Handover design did wrong, say what was fixed, and name the remaining piece as *"the separate deferred inverse-focus item, owned with the UI designer."*

**So the house pattern is: build to the project's standard, annotate the deviation inline citing the criterion and the source, and log the open item with the designer.** Which applied here means the stepper inherits the existing 24px, gets a comment naming 795's 44px AC and the 2.1-AAA-vs-2.2-AA mismatch, and goes on the designer's open list alongside the hover contrast and inverse focus ring already sitting there.

Annotated, not escalated. Moving on.

---

# Session notes — Cart bundle (SFCC-11), pre-build decisions

**Written:** 2026-09-16
**Branch at time of writing:** `feature/SFCC-831-689_country-language-mismatch` (NOT the build branch — a
fresh `feature/*` off `develop` is needed before any cart work starts)
**Scope:** card-by-card requirements pass over 7 Cart stories, ahead of a bundled build.
**Status:** all 7 cards read, all ACs pulled and adjudicated. No code written. No Jira updated.

The ACs do **not** live in the Jira description — they are in custom field `customfield_10231`
("Acceptance Criteria", project-scoped, textarea). Fetching only the description misses them
entirely. Some return plain text, some return ADF (`{type: "doc"}`) — SFCC-315/270/795 came back
as ADF and needed flattening.

---

## 1. The bundle

All 7 are Epic SFCC-11 (Cart), SFCC Sprint 5 (active, 2026-09-07 → 2026-09-21), label `Squad-A`,
assigned to Marcel, status **Ready for Development**.

| Card | Title | Priority | Reqs |
|---|---|---|---|
| SFCC-315 | Drawer Component (Cart Variation) – PWA Kit Component | High | CAI-006 |
| SFCC-270 | Cart Item Component UI (Part 1) – PWA Kit Component | High | CAI-006 |
| SFCC-795 | Cart Item Component UI (Part 2) – PWA Kit Component | Medium | — |
| SFCC-271 | Cart Item Component – Quantity Stepper | High | CAI-007 |
| SFCC-272 | Cart Item – Remove and Wishlist Actions | High | CAI-008, CAI-018 |
| SFCC-250 | Cart – Maximum Purchase Quantity Enforcement per SKU | Medium | CAI-017, PRD-011 |
| SFCC-275 | Cart Page – Button Group | High | CAI-010 |

### Bundle-shape decision

One gather pass and one plan across all 7 (done — this document). **Not** one mega-PR.
Rationale: a single PR converts 7 independently-mergeable units into one all-or-nothing unit;
one change-requested story would block the other six. Cart also spans two squads' Tier 2
ownership (`order-summary`/`promo-code` = Squad A, `product-item` = Squad B), so a single PR pulls
in both code-owner reviews at once, and AGENTS.md Hard Rule #10 requires explicit scope
confirmation before touching more than one protection tier in one change.

**Exception:** SFCC-250 and SFCC-272 are welded at the cart's `onAuthSuccess` seam (see §5) and
build as one PR. Accepted deliberately.

### A real CI consequence, not yet addressed

`qa.yml`'s `detect-changes` job has no **`cart`** e2e area. The existing areas are `homepage`,
`checkout`, `search`, `account`, `pdp`, `plp`, `integrations`. `e2e-localhost` only runs when every
e2e-relevant changed file falls inside exactly one area's allow-list — otherwise it resolves to
`e2e_scope: skip` and **does not run at all** on that PR. So every cart PR currently gets no
PR-time E2E. Adding a `cart` allow-list group + `@cart` tags is a deliberate step in the plan, not
something to discover afterwards. See `.claude/rules/testing.md` > Change-scoped E2E.

---

## 2. Verified findings (evidence-backed — re-verify before relying on any of these)

### 2.1 SFCC has no max-order-quantity field. The frontend constant IS the implementation.

- `commerce-sdk-isomorphic/lib/index.cjs.d.ts` contains `minOrderQuantity` (6 occurrences) and
  `stepQuantity`. **No `maxOrderQuantity` anywhere.**
- Live probe against the dev sandbox (site `ZimmermannAU`, shortCode `qmyt7hks`, SLAS private-client
  `client_credentials` guest token, mirroring `scripts/switchEnv.mjs`'s `liveCheckSfcc`), two real
  products: quantity-related keys returned are `inventory`, `minOrderQuantity`, `stepQuantity`.
  `maxOrderQuantity` absent.
- Custom attributes returned (so `c_*` exposure is working): `c_ap21Category`, `c_careInstructions`,
  `c_countryOfOrigin`, `c_environmentalNotes`, `c_fabricComposition`, `c_hsCode`, `c_isFinalSale`,
  `c_isNew`, `c_isSale`, `c_label`, `c_relatedMasterProductID`, `c_season`, `c_sizeFit`,
  `c_sizeGuide`, `c_styleId`, `c_styleNumber`, `c_stylingNotes`, `c_relatedSwatches`,
  `c_showEnvironmentalNote`. **None is a max-quantity attribute.**
- **Caveat:** dev sandbox only, 2 products. A custom attribute on sit/uat is not ruled out — but
  with no standard field at all, unlikely.
- `overrides/app/pages/product-detail/index.tsx:123`:
  `/** Frontend-enforced limit (SFCC-196). SFCC has no platform max-order-quantity field. */`
  `const MAX_PURCHASE_QUANTITY = 3;` — passed to `ProductView` as `maxOrderQuantity` at line 1282.
- **Conflict to record:** SFCC-268 "PDP – Maximum Purchase Quantity – **BM Config**" is
  *Ready for SIT* (Done, Sprint 3, Victor Crisostomo). Nothing reachable from the Shopper API was
  configured. 250's ACs all say "the **configured** maximum of 3".

### 2.2 The existing PDP enforcement shape (reusable)

`overrides/app/components/product-view/index.tsx`, `isMaxOrderQtyReached`:
```
if (maxOrderQuantity == null) return false;          // null = unrestricted
const inBag = basketProductItems
  .filter((item) => item.productId === productId)     // per SKU
  .reduce((sum, item) => sum + (item.quantity ?? 0), 0);  // summed ACROSS line items
return inBag >= maxOrderQuantity;                     // >=, not ==
```
Gates `handleAddToBag` (hard block) and caps `QuantityPicker`'s `max`. Tests/stories at 2, 3, null.
Note it **sums across line items** — i.e. the existing code already assumes one SKU can occupy more
than one line.

### 2.3 Basket merge: mode, default, and the same-product match rules

`mergeBasket` request parameter `productItemMergeMode`:
`"higher_quantity" | "sum_quantities" | "saved_quantity" | "separate_item"`.
SDK doc: *"By default, the higher of the two basket quantities is used for each product."*

Same-product match requires **all** of these to be equal:
> shipment · productId · option values · wishlist reference · inventory list id ·
> gift flag & message · ad-hoc price adjustments

> *"If any of the listed values don't match, then the item in the previous shopper's basket is
> copied to a **new line item** in the current shopper's basket."*

Consequence: `higher_quantity` protects only the single-line case. Two lines of the same SKU that
differ on shipment / inventory list / gift flag do **not** merge, and their quantities coexist —
so a SKU total can exceed the cap without any single line doing so. For Zimmermann the realistic
differentiators are **Collect in Boutique** (separate shipment) and **boutique vs warehouse
inventory lists** (CAI-022). At plain cart with no fulfilment choice made, both baskets sit in the
same default shipment and inventory list, so they DO match and 2 + 2 → 2 under the default.

### 2.4 Where merge is called, and with what

Four base call sites, **all passing only `createDestinationBasket: true`** (no merge mode):
- `node_modules/@salesforce/retail-react-app/app/hooks/use-auth-modal.js`
- `.../app/pages/login/index.jsx`
- `.../app/pages/social-login-redirect/index.jsx`
- `.../app/pages/checkout/partials/contact-info.jsx`

`use-auth-modal.js` carries the comment *"if you change logic here, also change it in login page"* —
Salesforce knows the invariant is duplicated.

**The invariant is login-only, deliberately not register:**
> *"we only want to merge basket when the user is logged in as a recurring user — only recurring
> users trigger the login mutation, new user triggers register mutation"*

Reason holds: a brand-new customer has no prior basket, so their guest basket simply becomes theirs.

### 2.5 No Zimmermann code merges baskets, and one route is a defect

- `grep -rn "mergeBasket" overrides/` → **empty.**
- `commerce-sdk-react` contains `mergeBasket` only as a mutation definition
  (`hooks/ShopperBaskets/mutation.js`), never in `auth/` — **the SDK does not auto-merge on login.**

`useWishlistAuthDrawer`'s three auth routes:

| Route | Merges? | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| Social IDP (`AuthorizeIDP`) | Yes — redirects through base `social-login-redirect`, which merges | ✅ fine |
| Create account (`useAuthModal(REGISTER_VIEW)`) | No — base deliberately skips register | ✅ correct by design |
| **Passwordless OTP (`LoginPasswordlessUser`)** | **No** | ❌ **DEFECT** |

Passwordless OTP is a recurring-user login, which is exactly the case the invariant exists for.
Base `use-auth-modal` has its own passwordless flow **and pairs it with the merge**;
`useWishlistAuthDrawer` reimplemented passwordless login for the drawer and did not carry the merge
across. Without a merge, SLAS switches the session to the registered customer and the guest basket
is orphaned — **the shopper's items are lost, not mis-counted.**

Affects all four consumers of the hook: the cart (new), `header/rightBar`, `drawer-menu`,
`product-view`.

**This is code-inferred, not yet observed live. Verify before filing** — guest adds an item, opens
the cart, signs in with the email code, check whether the item survives.

### 2.6 `PendingWishlistIntent` carries no product

`overrides/app/hooks/useWishlistAuthDrawer.ts`:
`type PendingWishlistIntent = { intentId: string; timestamp: number }`, session-stored under
`zimmPendingWishlistAction`, 5-minute max age, scoped by `intentId` so only the initiating instance
replays. Fine for the three existing callers (a PDP has one product; the header's action isn't
product-specific). **The cart is the first caller with N products**, so on the social-redirect route
the resumed `onAuthSuccess` has no idea which line item the shopper clicked.

### 2.7 No cart overrides exist at all

Absent: `overrides/app/pages/cart`, `overrides/app/components/cart`,
`overrides/app/components/order-summary`, `overrides/app/components/product-item`.
`overrides/app/pages/checkout` exists but contains only `partials/payment.tsx` + its story —
`contact-info` is **not** overridden.
No `overrides/app/pages/login` — base login page still in use.

### 2.8 Order summary updates for free

Base `pages/cart/index.jsx` calls `useCurrentBasket()`, mutates via
`updateItemInBasketMutation.mutateAsync`, and passes the same basket object to `<OrderSummary>`.
So "order summary updates when quantity changes" is a consequence of basket cache invalidation, not
code any stepper story owns. Base `components/order-summary/index.jsx` exists and has no override —
so SFCC-274 is "restyle it to Figma", not "build one that doesn't exist".

### 2.9 Base `product-item` is a shared SFCC internal

Imported by `components/product-item-list`, `pages/account/wishlist`, `pages/cart`.
`protectedFiles.md` puts `overrides/app/components/product-item/` at **Tier 2, Squad B-owned
(notify Squad A)**.

### 2.10 Base wishlist handler silently no-ops for guests

`pages/cart/index.jsx`, `handleAddToWishlist`:
```
if (!customerId || !wishlist) { return }
```
A guest clicking Move to Wishlist gets **nothing**. `cart.md` §2 (CAI-008) requires the opposite:
*"an unauthenticated user selecting Move to Wishlist is prompted to log in first."*
The same handler already implements the `isItemInWishlist` branch and surfaces success via a Chakra
toast (`TOAST_MESSAGE_ADDED_TO_WISHLIST`) with a "View Wishlist" action button.

### 2.11 ZimmButton variants and the 24px target size

Variants: `primary`, `primaryInverse`, `secondary`, `secondaryInverse`, `social`, `icon`,
`iconInverse`. Sizes: `lg`, `sm`, `social`, `icon`.
`sizes.icon` = `minW`/`minH: var(--zimm-scale-xl)`; `spacing.ts` resolves `xl` to `1.5rem` = **24px**,
chosen deliberately — the inline comment reads *"WCAG 2.2 AA SC 2.5.8 — 24px minimum target size.
SFCC-55's accessibility note names this control specifically."* It also explains why it is
`minW`/`minH` and not padding: Chakra's `IconButton` hard-sets `padding: 0` as a style prop, so
padding declared in the recipe is silently discarded (a previous `p: 'xs'` rendered 16×16).

`actionSizes.height` = `lg: 52px`, `md: 40px` (Figma-confirmed).
**`overrideStyling.md` is stale here:** it still cites `BTN_HEIGHT_LG`/`BTN_HEIGHT_SM`/`BTN_PADDING_Y`
as standing provisional exceptions. Those constants no longer exist in `zimmButton.css.ts`; the only
remaining provisional is `BTN_MIN_WIDTH_LG = '80px' // audit-allow: provisional`.

### 2.12 Domestic vs international is already modelled

`overrides/app/config/countries.ts`, `CountryConfig`:
`urlSlug`, `sfccSiteId`, `locale`, `currency`, `shippingCountry`, `checkoutOwner`, `globalEPricing`,
`boutiqueRegion`. `checkoutOwner`'s own doc comment:
> *"Checkout owner for this site's domestic path. Branch checkout AND pricing logic from this field
> at PDP/cart level — not only at the checkout page."*

Read via `overrides/app/hooks/useCountryConfig.ts` (matches on `sfccSiteId` + locale to disambiguate
the en-GB collision between the UK site and EU English; falls back to AU on an unrecognised site).

### 2.13 Base Checkout CTA has no region branch

`pages/cart/partials/cart-cta.jsx` → `<Button as={Link} to="/checkout">` unconditionally.
So international shoppers already land on SFCC checkout today; leaving that path alone is the
current behaviour, not a regression. The same file also uses `useExpressCheckoutEnabled()`, which
already gates express buttons on the cart — worth checking before writing new show/hide logic.

### 2.14 Empty-state precedent

`overrides/app/pages/recentlyViewed/index.tsx` (on `origin/feature/SFCC-83-84_recently-viewed-einstein`,
PR #116 — **not merged to develop**). Pattern, per its own JSDoc: structure ported from base
`EmptyCart` (`pages/cart/partials/empty-cart.jsx`) as `Box > Center > Stack`; `isRegistered`-branched
body copy; `Button as={Link}` using the **base SFCC `Link`** (not raw react-router) so the CTA href
gets multi-site prefixing via `use-multi-site`'s `buildUrl`; `useIntl` called directly in the leaf
under the Context-backed exception in `components.md`; private single-parent sub-component so no
story/test of its own; decision log at the bottom of the file.

That file made **autonomous styling judgement calls** because it had no design at all. The cart
does have one (SFCC-315 carries an Empty Cart screenshot), so take **structure** from the precedent
and **visuals from Figma** — do not repeat the token-invention.

### 2.15 House pattern for a design-vs-standard deviation

From `zimmButton.css.ts`: cite the specific criterion, name where the requirement came from, explain
any mechanical gotcha, and name what is deferred and who owns it. Examples in that file: the 2.5.8
note above, and the focus-ring block — *"Replaces the previous outline:none + bg-swap, which gave the
primary variant an invisible focus state (#191919 default vs #000000 focus) — a WCAG 2.4.7 failure...
Dark-surface / inverse ring (grey-white) is the separate deferred inverse-focus item, owned with the
UI designer."*

**Annotate inline, log with the designer, ship. Do not escalate or block.**

---

## 3. A reading correction worth keeping

I over-read cross-references three times in this session. A `see SFCC-NNN` / "Relates to" in an AC
usually points at **where the design or detail lives**, not at a gate. Treat it as a dependency only
when the card says so outright — as SFCC-272's description does (*"This story is dependent on other
components being developed, including..."*) and SFCC-250's does (*"The following components must be
developed before this story can be implemented end to end"*).

Wrongly called blocked and later corrected: SFCC-271 (on 274), SFCC-275 (on 816), and AC2 of
SFCC-272 (on 277).

---

## 4. Per-card decisions

### SFCC-315 — Drawer (Cart Variation) · 9 ACs · all buildable

ACs: header `"BAG • [count]"` with right-aligned X / `"YOUR BAG IS EMPTY"` when empty; count updates
dynamically without reload; slides in from the right, right portion on desktop+tablet with a
non-interactive overlaid background, **full screen on mobile**; closes via X, outside click, and
Escape with **focus returned to the trigger**; no loss of page state or scroll position on close;
responsive per Figma.

- Build as a **new organism wrapping `ZimmDrawer`**, not as a modification to the atom and not as an
  override of base `pages/cart`.
- Reuse: `ZimmDrawer` already has `finalFocusRef` (AC7), the overlay, right placement, size variants,
  mobile full-height, and concurrent-instance scroll-lock coordination — all from SFCC-831/926.
- AC3's dynamic count comes free from basket cache invalidation.
- AC8: verify the scroll-lock **restores** position on close rather than merely unlocking.
- **315 owns the empty-state *header text* only.** The empty *body* is SFCC-277's. Clean split.
- 315 is a dependency for SFCC-270, 274, 316, 318, 404 — and **SFCC-316 (Zimmermann Benefits –
  Contentful) is Sprint 5, Ready for Development, assigned to Jhoan Rose Dela Cruz.** Someone else's
  active-sprint card is waiting on this. **Ship 315 first and standalone.**

### SFCC-270 — Cart Item UI Part 1 · 9 ACs · all buildable

ACs: per line item — image; name to the right of the image; price; selected colour; selected size;
quantity with `+`/`–` either side; multiple items each individually identifiable; Remove and Wishlist
as **underlined text links below the stepper**; on mobile nothing truncated or hidden.

**Open architectural decision (not settled):** override base `product-item` vs build a new
`ZimmCartItem` organism.
- Override → Tier 2, Squad B-owned; default export must stay API-compatible for `pages/cart`,
  `pages/account/wishlist` and `product-item-list` (the SFCC bridge pattern in `overrideStyling.md`);
  Zimmermann styling goes in a theme recipe.
- New organism → stays in Squad A's territory, no compatibility constraint, coherent with 315 being
  a new organism. **Cost:** the account wishlist page keeps base styling, so cart and wishlist line
  items will look different until that page is done.

### SFCC-271 — Quantity Stepper · 4 ACs · all buildable

ACs: `+` increments by 1 with item total and order summary updating; `–` decrements when quantity > 1;
at quantity 1 the `–` is disabled and quantity stays 1; drawer count (`Bag 3`) and order summary both
update without a full page load.

- **No SFCC-274 dependency** — see §2.8. Deliverable is the mutation call, the debounce, the
  optimistic local quantity, and the error rollback. The summary updating falls out of invalidation.
- Courtesy heads-up to Hazel (SFCC-274's assignee): the stepper lands first and sets the
  invalidation contract; the order summary should read basket state via `useCurrentBasket()` rather
  than holding its own copy.

### SFCC-795 — Cart Item UI Part 2 · the largest card

Groups: default state (restates 270); stepper states (quantity 1 → `–` disabled/greyed; > 1 → both
enabled; at max → `+` disabled/greyed; fully OOS or unavailable → **both** disabled/greyed); error
state (red inline message beneath the stepper — OOS, Partially OOS, Unavailable, copy supplied);
promotional price ("Was $X" / "Now $Y" replacing standard price, plus a discount label beneath the
stepper e.g. "20% off applied"); warning state (grey info icon + message, e.g. "Maximum purchase
quantity reached for this size"); responsive; and **11 accessibility ACs**.

Decisions:
- **Overlap with 270/271/250 is intentional layering — build once, satisfy all.** This is the
  explicit reason for bundling. Consequence to accept: the ACs can't be signed off independently and
  Zephyr will count the same coverage from three keys.
- **Error states: presentation here, triggering logic elsewhere.** OOS / Partially OOS belong to

`overrides/app/components/product-view/index.tsx`, `isMaxOrderQtyReached`:
```
if (maxOrderQuantity == null) return false;          // null = unrestricted
const inBag = basketProductItems
  .filter((item) => item.productId === productId)     // per SKU
  .reduce((sum, item) => sum + (item.quantity ?? 0), 0);  // summed ACROSS line items
return inBag >= maxOrderQuantity;                     // >=, not ==
```
Gates `handleAddToBag` (hard block) and caps `QuantityPicker`'s `max`. Tests/stories at 2, 3, null.
Note it **sums across line items** — i.e. the existing code already assumes one SKU can occupy more

### 2.3 Basket merge: mode, default, and the same-product match rules

`mergeBasket` request parameter `productItemMergeMode`:
`"higher_quantity" | "sum_quantities" | "saved_quantity" | "separate_item"`.
SDK doc: *"By default, the higher of the two basket quantities is used for each product."*

Same-product match requires **all** of these to be equal:
> shipment · productId · option values · wishlist reference · inventory list id ·
> gift flag & message · ad-hoc price adjustments

> *"If any of the listed values don't match, then the item in the previous shopper's basket is
> copied to a **new line item** in the current shopper's basket."*

Consequence: `higher_quantity` protects only the single-line case. Two lines of the same SKU that
differ on shipment / inventory list / gift flag do **not** merge, and their quantities coexist —
so a SKU total can exceed the cap without any single line doing so. For Zimmermann the realistic
differentiators are **Collect in Boutique** (separate shipment) and **boutique vs warehouse
inventory lists** (CAI-022). At plain cart with no fulfilment choice made, both baskets sit in the
same default shipment and inventory list, so they DO match and 2 + 2 → 2 under the default.

Four base call sites, **all passing only `createDestinationBasket: true`** (no merge mode):
- `node_modules/@salesforce/retail-react-app/app/hooks/use-auth-modal.js`
- `.../app/pages/login/index.jsx`
- `.../app/pages/social-login-redirect/index.jsx`
- `.../app/pages/checkout/partials/contact-info.jsx`

`use-auth-modal.js` carries the comment *"if you change logic here, also change it in login page"* —
Salesforce knows the invariant is duplicated.

**The invariant is login-only, deliberately not register:**
> *"we only want to merge basket when the user is logged in as a recurring user — only recurring
> users trigger the login mutation, new user triggers register mutation"*

Reason holds: a brand-new customer has no prior basket, so their guest basket simply becomes theirs.

warning is 795's, the page-level banner is 404's.

| Decision | Value |
|---|---|
| Max value | No BM setting exists (§2.1). Promote `MAX_PURCHASE_QUANTITY` out of `product-detail/index.tsx:123` into a shared constant; cart reads the same one. Re-typing `3` would breach `conventions.md`'s no-magic-numbers rule. |
| Threshold | **`>=`**, not the AC's literal "equals" — otherwise a line already holding 4 fails the check and the `+` stays live exactly when it matters. Matches the PDP. |
| Scope of the limit | **Per line item.** Rationale: the SKU is already size *and* colour, so in normal shopping one line **is** one SKU. |
| Merge mode | **`sum_quantities`.** AC5's "combined quantity ... exceeds the maximum" only works if quantities add. |
| Cap shape | **Consolidate to one line at 3.** Free — `sum_quantities` already produces a single *"merged line item"* for matching products. |
| Merge call | **Zimmermann-owned**, placed where `loginPasswordless.mutateAsync` succeeds in `useWishlistAuthDrawer` — completing the half-implemented pairing in §2.5, and covering all four consumers at once. |
| Callback order | **merge → cap → 272's pending wishlist resume.** The wishlist move acts on a line the merge may have just consolidated and the cap just reduced; reversing the order moves a quantity the shopper never saw. |
| Render guard | Secondary backstop for baskets that went over some other way (stale session, order-on-behalf). **No-ops while any basket mutation is in flight** via React Query's `useIsMutating()`, so it cannot race the callback. |
| Shared logic | Merge-and-cap lives in **its own small function**, called by both the callback and the render guard — one implementation, not two copies. |
| Flash (briefly showing 4) | **No action.** Observe the real behaviour first. |
| Loop guard | **Keep it** — distinct from the flash. Without it, a write-on-render can fire repeatedly (concurrent writes racing on one line item; or endless retries if the server refuses), which can rate-limit a shopper out of their own basket. One correction in flight, one attempt per basket version, then stop and surface an error. |

AC disposition: **1, 2** build (needs 271, 795) · **3, 8** → SFCC-404 · **4, 9** nothing to build
(negative assertions; Apple/Google Pay buttons don't exist yet anyway) · **5** build ·
**6, 7** free — they are AC1 and AC2's rules applied to a post-merge state, and a consolidated line
at 3 satisfies per-line `>=`.

**Accepted consequence of `sum_quantities`, recorded deliberately:** it changes **every** merge, not
just over-max ones. A guest adds one dress, signs in a week later, the account already had it —
today they get one, with summing they get two. Marcel accepted this explicitly. **It must go in a
comment on the card**, because no AC describes it and a tester finding it otherwise has no way to
know two items is intended rather than a bug.

**Deliberate boundary, recorded so it isn't mistaken for an oversight:** per-line enforcement means
a SKU split across two lines can total more than 3 without either line hitting max. That case only
arises from the merge splitting a line, which is what AC5 exists to catch. In that same edge case the
PDP (which sums per SKU) and the cart (per line) apply different rules.

Verified 2026-09-16 against `commerce-sdk-isomorphic` types and the base template.

**`mergeBasket`'s `productItemMergeMode`** is `higher_quantity` (default) | `sum_quantities` |
`saved_quantity` | `separate_item`. Default means **guest 2 + account 2 → 2, not 4** — quantities
never sum unless the mode is passed explicitly, and it can only be passed at the call site.

**Same-product matching** requires all of: shipment · productId · option values · wishlist
reference · inventory list id · gift flag & message · ad-hoc price adjustments. Any mismatch
copies the item to a **new line item** instead of merging — so one SKU can exceed a per-order cap
across two lines without either line doing so. For Zimmermann the realistic differentiators are
Collect in Boutique (separate shipment) and boutique vs warehouse inventory lists.

**Four base call sites**, all passing only `createDestinationBasket: true`: `hooks/use-auth-modal`,
`pages/login`, `pages/social-login-redirect`, `pages/checkout/partials/contact-info`. The merge is
deliberately **login-only, not register** — a new customer's guest basket simply becomes theirs.

**No Zimmermann code calls `mergeBasket`**, and `commerce-sdk-react` does not auto-merge (it only
defines the mutation). Of `useWishlistAuthDrawer`'s three routes: social redirects through the base
page that merges; create-account correctly skips it; **passwordless OTP merges nothing** — so a
recurring shopper signing in that way has their guest basket orphaned and **loses their items**.
Code-inferred, not yet observed live — prove it before filing.

**Why:** any cart/checkout work touching sign-in inherits this. Assuming the server sums, or
assuming a merge happens at all, both produce silently wrong baskets.

**How to apply:** check what mode a merge call passes before reasoning about quantities, and treat
"a guest signed in" as "the basket may have been orphaned" until the passwordless gap is fixed.
Related: [[project-cart-bundle-decisions]], [[project-max-order-quantity]].
EOF
